items.title: How the Democrats Beat Trump
items.description: C ampaigns are billion-dollar contests to define the choice facing voters, but no election season this century has closed quite like this. President Trump approached his task with sarcasm and shiny objects, asking voters desperate for financial help to think only of him. If Republicans did not vote, they would “go to hell,” he said with a smile. If Republicans won the House and Senate, they would get a $5,000 check that even some of his allies dismissed as fiscal absurdity. Then he told them stories, endless stories, for hours at a time—about rounded butts, strong hands, “Dumocrats,” transgender swim meets, the Vietnam War, and the blue paint he had reapplied to the Reflecting Pool. “At this point, they are not even trying,” one Republican consultant told us about the White House in the final days of the campaign. Trump would do it his way, just as the Frank Sinatra song on the president’s iPad playlist advises. Hakeem Jeffries, the next House speaker, answered Trump’s Borscht Belt tour with relentless repetition. He declared on Fox News last month that “costs are way too high” just hours before Trump interrupted a campaign rally to ogle what he’s called the “pile of muscle” on the rump of Ohio’s junior senator. Days later, Jeffries pledged yet again that Democrats would “relentlessly focus” on affordability while Trump boasted about the nation “making a fortune” from rising gas prices. After the president joked about the high cost of a hamburger at Mar-a-Lago, Jeffries listed his priorities as “housing, health care, and the cost of gas and groceries and goods.” The New York congressman delivered the same message nearly every day—precise paragraphs punctuated with syncopated gesticulation and excessive alliteration. Rarely had two men atop the political pyramid been more opposite. In place of Trump’s billionaire power suits and cascading bouffant, Jeffries dressed in the capsule wardrobe of middle management, his white-soled dress sneakers unscuffed, his hair always trimmed a millimeter or two shy of a clean shave. By the final days of the campaign, the Democratic leader could barely contain his delight. “They’re talking about ballrooms and body parts,” Jeffries told a roundtable of Black pastors outside Richmond, Virginia, last week while campaigning in a district that Trump won by five points two years ago. “It’s more of the same—extremism, foolishness, and corruption—or it’s dramatic change.” Tonight Democrats won control of the House and the Senate—and vindicated the discipline of Jeffries and his fellow Democrats. But they didn’t pull it off alone. They received extraordinary help from Trump, whose tariffs and protracted conflict with Iran juiced inflation, and whose obsession with building and profit-taking rattled voters. In two short years, Democrats have reclaimed the economic issues they lost on in 2024, and Trump has squandered the confidence of his winning majority. For the first time since 2014, public polling shows that Democrats are more trusted on the economy than Republicans. This story, about how that transformation unfolded, is based on interviews with 15 people involved in the inner workings of the campaigns on either side of the aisle. At its most basic, Democrats did what they needed by maintaining a tight focus, something Trump either believed was not necessary—or was not capable of achieving. “We had to remain committed to keeping the main thing the main thing,” Jeffries told us a few days before Election Day, during some downtime between campaign stops. “If we were going to reverse our political fortunes we had to convince the American people that we were determined to make their life more affordable . ” Two months earlier, Jeffries gathered Democratic lawmakers in the Capitol for a slide-deck presentation that quantified how their focus was paying off. He showed them April polling data from Blue Rose Research, a Democratic firm, that ranked cost of living, the economy, inflation, and health care as the first, second, third, and sixth top voter concerns. Then he showed them the problem: Voters credited Democrats with making health care the top issue but listed nine priorities they believed Democrats placed ahead of the economy, and 14 priorities before inflation. Jeffries clicked to the next slide, an August poll result on the same questions demonstrating that Democrats had found the solution: an almost perfect alignment between voter and party priorities. Cost of living, the economy, inflation, and health care now ranked as the top four issues, in order. Voters had come to believe that Democrats were focused most on the cost of living, followed by health care as No. 2, the economy as No. 3, and inflation coming in at No. 5. Senate strategists were seeing the same data and arguing for the same approach, especially as winning the chamber became more of a possibility. “There was a very simple solution to say, Guys, there’s an out-of-control affordability crisis that Democrats kind of missed the boat on, for whatever reason, to varying degrees in 2024 , so we need to focus like a laser on that now, ” Matt Canter, a Democratic strategist, told us. “Paying for gas persuades people.” One of the most remarkable ads of the 2024 campaign cycle was a Trump attack on misplaced Democratic priorities. The spot focused on Vice President Harris’s support for taxpayer-funded sex-change operations in prisons, with a searing tagline: “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.” Two years later, Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic consultant, noticed how the dynamic had inverted. Trump was defending unpopular data-center construction and Flock surveillance cameras. His final televised address before Election Day was on the National Mall, not in a key battleground state, and focused on the Triumphal Arch and the new golf course he planned along the Potomac River. “Republicans are focused on he/him,” Ferguson told us, “and Democrats are focused on you.” T he Democrats’ journey to reclaiming majorities in the House and Senate began as soon as Trump arrived back in Washington, D.C. Two weeks after Trump’s second inauguration, Jeffries described the Democratic problem as one of connection. “Maya Angelou said it best: People won’t remember what you say. They may not even remember what you do. But they will always remember how you make them feel,” he said on the comedian Jon Stewart’s podcast. “And I think what we have to do a better job of is making the American people feel that we understand the pain that they’ve been in economically for a long period of time.” In Jeffries’ telling, economic anxiety was the leading political issue for the past four decades. Seeking relief, voters had ping-ponged between ideologies and parties—electing George H. W. Bush, Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Trump, Joe Biden, and then Trump again. “What’s consistent? The American people have a constant desire for change,” he said. “Why? Because no one has solved the fundamental problem.” [ Read: The states where Democrats have the most to gain ] By that point, House Majority PAC, the independent group affiliated with Jeffries, had already done a deep dive into the 2024 results, asking for an analysis of every public remark and paid communication in each contested congressional race. The clear result: The more a candidate talked about the economy, the better they performed. What mattered most was the frequency of talking about voters’ top concern. When Democratic pollsters asked voters to pick between a binary of economic concerns and any other issue—such as crime, immigration, abortion, foreign policy, regulation—the economic concerns were chosen by 75 to 95 percent of voters. “We lost because Democrats were perceived to be out of alignment” in 2024, Mike Smith, the president of the House Majority PAC, told us. Within weeks of the podcast taping, Jeffries and his top advisers received more sobering news: Democrats were being overwhelmed by the shock and awe of Trump’s second term—the pardoning of the January 6 rioters, the mass firing of civil servants , the closure of whole government agencies, the immigration raids, the obsequiousness of corporate leaders, the remaking of the global order. A Democratic consultant arrived with voter research that showed the average American paid attention to politics for about four minutes a week, and three minutes and 30 seconds were focused on what Trump was doing. At best, Democrats were competing for 30 seconds every seven days—about .007 percent of an average voter’s waking hours. Jeffries concluded that Democrats could not compete on Trump’s terms. The president’s megaphone would blare louder. “We always understood simplicity and repetition is the only way to break through,” Jeffries told us about the challenge presented by Trump. “It quickly became apparent to me that the downside of his strategy, as long as we didn’t fall for it, was that the American people would conclude, Well, I may not be following all of the craziness that’s being unleashed on us, but I do know he ain’t focused on the thing that he promised he would focus on, which is to lower our costs .” The wisdom of this plan was not always obvious to Jeffries’ caucus. The dramatic cuts by the Department of Government Efficiency led some lawmakers to demand a defense of government institutions. The abuses of immigration enforcement created constant outrage. The attacks on media outlets and university independence rattled constitutional scholars. But Jeffries demanded that the caucus find a script and stick to it. When Trump pushed through his summer tax bill last year, Jeffries urged the caucus to focus on the Medicaid cuts it would force—a proxy for the help that working people needed—even though some Democrats argued that such a message could be attacked as a defense of poverty entitlements. By the late summer, with Obamacare subsidies set to expire at the end of the year, Democratic leaders settled on a strategy of forcing a government shutdown. The question was why. Ezra Klein, the New York Times columnist closely read by the Democratic rank and file in Congress, urged Democrats to make the shutdown about a broad range of things that were no longer normal—not just rising costs but also Trump’s corruption and authoritarian impulses. At a Democratic caucus meeting days later, Jeffries faced a divided party, including those sympathetic to Klein’s argument that the party needed to go big. But the leader pushed back, saying it should focus on only one issue: health-care costs. “It’s the right fight, and it’s a good fight,” he told his members, before quoting the late Vernon Johns, a mentor to Martin Luther King Jr.: “If you see a good fight, get in it.” Klein told us that he came to admire Jeffries’s judgement, even if it contradicted his advice at the time. “He chose his shutdown, and he won his shutdown, and that is pretty rare for the minority party,” Klein said. “I think the Democrats have done a good job listening broadly to the public rather than narrowly to people who just vote for Democrats.” Several Democrats told us that they also credit Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, as well as the party at large, for staying unified, both during the shutdown and throughout the remainder of the election cycle. A Democratic pollster told us that the Democratic coordination was not just a happy accident. “It was the result of a lot of advance planning, a lot of outreach to various stakeholder groups,” this person said. Lauren French, the communications director for Senate Majority PAC, the independent group affiliated with Senate Democratic leaders, told us that the major role Schumer played in candidate recruitment proved crucial; he helped persuade Mary Peltola in Alaska, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, and Sherrod Brown in Ohio to run, and he was also supportive of Josh Turek ’s candidacy in Iowa and James Talarico’s candidacy in Texas. Cooper proved so strong that Democrats could pull money from North Carolina and use it elsewhere. Trump, meanwhile, went in the opposite direction. He helped push out Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican, clearing the way for the Democratic pickup. He undercut Texas’s incumbent senator, John Cornyn, in favor of a troubled candidate, Ken Paxton, who had been impeached by his own party and faced other scandals. Republicans soon had to redirect hundreds of millions more to a state that hadn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly 40 years. Paxton then lost, as did Texas Governor Greg Abbott. After the unexpected death of Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina this summer, Trump selected Darline Graham, a political novice with none of her brother’s foreign-policy expertise, to replace him. Graham struggled on the campaign trail, prompting claims that she was a “nepo sister”—and yesterday, South Carolina elected a Democratic senator for the first time in more than two decades. Since the start of his term, Trump’s approval rating has been on steady decline. But the sharpest dips in 2025 coincided with particular presidential actions: in April, weeks after Trump announced his tariff regime; in July, weeks after Trump passed his tax bill; in November, around the end of the government shutdown and a House vote on releasing the investigative files of the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Epstein scandal, Democrats realized over time, was unexpectedly tied to economic insecurity. It fed into a broader concern that elites were operating by a different set of rules. Trump’s ballroom and allegations of improper stock trading by Republicans in Congress fit within that narrative. At the House Majority PAC, strategists realized that they could turn corruption into a cost–of-living argument— things are expensive , they began telling their ad makers, because the system is rigged . “Corruption is not an abstract thing,” one Jeffries adviser told us, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe private strategy. “It is not about systems and not about institutions. It is about you and your life.” [ Read: The Republicans are bolting from Trump ] Democrats already felt they were on the right path, but then, at the end of February, Trump launched a war against Iran that spiked gas prices and again pushed inflation higher. Jeffries pushed for an immediate vote to put Democrats on record in opposition, and Republicans on record in support. Then he began the argument that this, too, would be a fight about pocketbook issues, not abstract debates about geopolitics, collateral damage by the U.S. military, a war for oil, or whether Trump was usurping the Constitution by not requesting a formal declaration of war from Congress. As the war dragged on, Republican hopes collapsed. The clearest correlation in politics in 2026 was between gas prices at the pump and the generic ballot advantage of Democrats. “All of the polling couldn’t be more clear,” a Republican consultant told us. “We were on track towards a normal midterm map prior to the war, and you can see the favorability numbers for the administration, for Republicans at large, take a nosedive after the war began.” Another Democratic polling operation this year asked a broader question: Regardless of what you want from the election results, would you rather things stay the same as they are now or change? Eighty-five percent of voters chose change, and only 6 percent went with the status quo. The potential was enormous. “People are willing to accept change over their party controlling Congress,” Jon Fromowitz, a co-founder of the Democratic group Future Forward, told us. “People were upset enough about the way things were going that they were very open-minded.” T he only time that Jeffries and Trump formally met in person was a trap. Jeffries and Schumer were invited to the Oval Office last September, and Jeffries walked in concerned that television cameras would be there to film a staged confrontation that could rival Trump’s showdown months earlier with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. As it happened, Trump had something else in mind. He started by offering the Democrats Diet Cokes. When they declined, the sodas were delivered anyway and placed on the Resolute Desk. Then an adviser came in and put red Trump 2028 hats next to the drinks. As they debated the terms of the coming shutdown battle with House Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a photographer started circling them to get shots of Jeffries with the hats in the frame. “It was the strangest thing ever,” Jeffries said afterward, trying to explain the experience to CNN. After Jeffries left for a press conference with Schumer outside the West Wing, Trump posted a video that had added animated Mexican sombreros on their heads. Now, more than a year later, Jeffries is poised to become the leader of the House, and the first Black lawmaker to hold the position. Democrats will be able to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses, but they will still operate under the threat of a presidential veto and a 60-vote cloture rule in the Senate that will require bipartisan cooperation. As it stands, Jeffries and Trump have almost no relationship. After Trump posted a racist video that animated Barack and Michelle Obama as monkeys, Jeffries filmed his own reaction in a video in which he said, “Fuck Donald Trump.” (Trump deleted the Obama video and blamed staff for posting it.) The president has called the man who will be house speaker “lunatic, Hakeem ‘Low IQ’ Jeffries” and called for his prosecution. [ Read: Here’s who Democrats want to impeach next ] Jeffries has argued for months that animosity toward Trump will not interfere with Democrats’ unified focus on lowering costs. He has pointed to a bipartisan housing-affordability bill, sponsored by liberal Democrats in the House and Senate, that passed in June, with 191 Democratic votes and 166 Republican votes. A more cynical party in an election year might have denied Republicans the chance for an affordability win in the summer, but Democrats moved ahead anyway, creating what Jeffries now believes can be a model. “Our view was do the right thing, and we’ll just deal with the politics of it when we have to deal with the politics of it,” Jeffries told us. “We’re running on affordability, we’re gonna win on affordability, and we have to govern on affordability.” Democratic success also comes with notes of caution. There is a difference between winning a referendum against the status quo and winning the confidence of the American people to chart a new path forward. Democrats have the advantage on polls of economic trust because the Republican brand has fallen so far, not because the Democratic one has risen much. “I think Trump lost it,” the Democratic pollster told us, noting that polls still show no meaningful increase in the favorability of the Democratic Party. At the same time, even those closest to Trump in the White House are hesitant to guess how he will react in the weeks ahead. The president has no record of taking responsibility for failure, and he regularly lashes out at others when things go wrong. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he posted on social media once his defeat had become clear. The official message from the White House was defiance and a recommitment to fight. But White House advisers have begun talking, quietly for now, about the “populist” issues they could get behind in the last two years of Trump’s term that would get Democratic support. Trump’s decision to create savings accounts for all American children began in the 1990s as a Democratic idea, called “KidSave,” a version of which was supported by President Bill Clinton’s administration. Hillary Clinton, in her 2008 campaign for president, proposed a similar “Baby Bonds” account. Trump’s team has been making plans to build upon them in the coming months. But Republicans now face the same project that Democrats faced following sharp spikes in inflation under Biden: a sprint to get back on the right side of a voting majority, with only one issue at play. It is not a problem that will be easily fixed by mean tweets and diversion. It is also not a fight that Democrats are going to cede like Trump did over the last year. After it was clear that voters had delivered Democrats control of the House, Jeffries took the stage at a victory party in Washington. “We are going to fight to make sure that we make this country affordable for every single American,” he said. “We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you beginning on day one.” Behind him was a printed backdrop with the message he had repeated hundreds of times— Fighting for an Affordable America . Simplicity and repetition had won the day.

items.title: Fidelity Bank becomes Ghana’s only bank to achieve 2X Certified Advanced status for gender-smart finance
items.description: Fidelity Bank Ghana has achieved 2X Certified Advanced status, becoming the only bank in Ghana to attain this distinction and reinforcing its commitment to advancing gender-smart finance and women’s economic empowerment. Awarded by 2X Global, the global industry organisation that promotes gender-smart investing, the certification recognises the Bank’s efforts to integrate gender considerations into its leadership, employment practices, products and services, and investment portfolio. The achievement follows Fidelity Bank’s participation in the 2025–2026 pilot of the new 2X Certification methodology for financial institutions, led by 2X Global. The pilot assessed the methodology across different financial institution business models and incorporated practical insights and feedback to strengthen the framework ahead of its launch on 3 November 2026. 2X Certification provides a framework for assessing financial institutions’ commitment to gender equality and women’s economic empowerment through demonstrable practices across their businesses. A key achievement for Fidelity Bank was its Products and Services offering, which met the certification’s Best-in-Class requirement. This recognises the Bank’s efforts to integrate gender considerations into product development, delivery, customer service and marketing, while responding to the distinct financial needs of women and girls. These efforts include establishing Women’s Desks to support women customers, the Fidelity Young Entrepreneurs Initiative, the Edwapa Account, the Fidelity Bright Kids Account, the Education Support Plan, and digital banking solutions tailored to women’s financial needs and preferences. Together, these initiatives reflect the Bank’s commitment to expanding access to financial services and developing relevant solutions that support girls, women and their businesses. Beyond its products and services, Fidelity Bank has strengthened its approach to gender inclusion through strategic partnerships. The Bank engaged Value for Women, with support from AfricInvest and BIO Invest, to provide targeted technical assistance towards advancing gender inclusion. The engagement included a gender diagnostic to identify challenges and opportunities within the Bank, a workshop to review findings and explore potential interventions, and a tailored Gender Action Plan to guide the implementation of prioritised initiatives. Additionally, funding from Fidelity Bank’s partnership with Accion International supported an MSME Needs Assessment conducted with Ipsos, the development of a Women’s Intentionality Roadmap in 2024, the development of a Gender Policy and the recruitment of a Gender Specialist. These initiatives helped institutionalise gender-responsiveness into the Bank’s core practices, deepen its understanding of the needs of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises and identify opportunities to make its financial solutions more responsive to women’s needs. Commenting on the achievement, Atta Yeboah Gyan, Deputy Managing Director, Operations & Support Functions, at Fidelity Bank Ghana, said: “Achieving 2X Certified Advanced status is an important milestone for Fidelity Bank and a strong endorsement of the deliberate steps we are taking to embed gender inclusion across our business. We believe that empowering women and expanding economic opportunities for girls and women are not just social priorities; they are essential to building stronger businesses, communities and economies. “Being the only bank in Ghana to attain this distinction is a proud moment for us. It also reinforces our responsibility to keep raising the bar by developing relevant financial solutions, creating opportunities for women-owned and women-led businesses, and fostering an inclusive workplace. “We remain committed to ensuring that girls, women and their businesses have greater opportunities to participate in and contribute to economic growth.” The 2X Certification reinforces Fidelity Bank’s broader commitment to sustainability and responsible business practices, marks an important milestone in this journey, and strengthens the Bank’s resolve to advance gender equality, expand access to finance, and support inclusive economic growth.

items.title: Asiedu Nketia has earned the right to contest for president — Fifi Kwetey
items.description: The General Secretary of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Fifi Kwetey, has thrown his weight behind the right of the party’s National Chairman, Johnson Asiedu Nketia, to contest the presidency, saying his years of dedicated service to the party make him qualified to seek the highest political office. He said there was nothing objectionable about Mr Asiedu Nketia pursuing a presidential ambition, should he decide to enter the race. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, November 3, Mr Kwetey described the NDC chairman as a committed party stalwart who had served the organisation diligently and deserved the opportunity to seek the presidency. “It shouldn’t be a problem at all. I mean, he qualifies to run for president,” he said. Mr Kwetey added that Mr Asiedu Nketia’s long service to the party, including his leadership at the highest levels, should not be a basis for denying him the opportunity to contest. “Of course. I mean, he has served the party diligently. I mean, at the highest level, if he wants to go for it, should I call it the highest position of the party, why not?” he said. Fair contest for all However, the NDC General Secretary was careful not to declare support for Mr Asiedu Nketia’s possible presidential bid, insisting that his responsibility was to ensure a level playing field for all prospective candidates. He said the party’s leadership must strengthen the NDC as a political organisation and create conditions under which every qualified aspirant could freely pursue their ambitions. Mr Kwetey said the eventual choice of a presidential candidate should rest with party members rather than individual leaders. “For me, it’s not about support; at the moment, my job for now is to ensure that the party as a vehicle remains strong and ensure that we create a fair playing field for everybody and then let the party make that determination as to where next we ought to go,” he said. He stressed that he would not impose his personal preference on the party, adding that the decision must emerge from the collective judgement of its members. “So it will not be my choice at all. It will be the choice of the masses. And our people are very discerning,” he said. Mr Kwetey’s comments come amid discussions within the NDC about possible contenders for the party’s next presidential flagbearer election. Mr Asiedu Nketia, popularly known as General Mosquito, has held several key positions in the party, including General Secretary and National Chairman. His possible entry into the presidential contest would add another prominent figure to the conversation about the party’s future leadership.

items.title: Burkina Faso: Islamist Armed Group Targets Civilians
items.description: Click to expand Image Ouahigouya, Burkina Faso, October 25, 2021. © 2021 Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty Images An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso’s northern Yatenga province in September 2026.The group’s relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, and those who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes.Burkina Faso authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible. (Nairobi) – An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso’s northern Yatenga province in September 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. These attacks violated international humanitarian law and are apparent war crimes. On September 1, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM) attacked a gold mining site in Soubo, Ouahigouya district, killing 24 civilians, injuring at least 20 others, and burning property. On September 5, three civilians on a motorcycle, including a child, were killed by an explosive weapon on a dirt track near Mera village, also in Ouahigouya district. Local residents believe JNIM forces had planted an improvised explosive device (IED). “The JNIM armed group’s relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible.” Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch. In September and October, Human Rights Watch remotely interviewed 15 people, including 4 witnesses to the Soubo attack and 3 to the Mera attack, as well as human rights defenders and journalists. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated four videos posted online showing the aftermath of the Soubo attack and analyzed satellite imagery and fire detection data to corroborate witness accounts. On September 1 at about 1 a.m., over 60 JNIM fighters riding motorbikes stormed an artisanal gold mining site about 1.5 kilometers northwest of Soubo village. They fired on civilians sleeping and working there, and at those trying to flee. “I’ve seen dozens of injured people, many by bullets, others because they fell while fleeing and fractured their legs or arms,” a 45-year-old man said. He said that those with gunshot wounds were treated at the regional university hospital in Ouahigouya. Witnesses said the attack lasted about two hours. Fearing further attacks, residents stayed away from the site for two to three days. During the attack, JNIM fighters destroyed hundreds of temporary structures such as sheds and huts, as well as motorcycles and mining tools. JNIM’s Sharia Committee, in a September 30 response (English, Arabic) to Human Rights Watch, acknowledged that JNIM forces attacked Soubo, but stated that the victims were members of the government-allied militias, known as Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie, or VDP) and “not civilians.” However, witnesses told Human Rights Watch that soldiers and VDPs were neither present during the attack nor stationed at the site, although they occasionally patrolled the surrounding area. Mining sites are lucrative revenue sources for JNIM in Burkina Faso. The armed group leverages mining economies to generate revenue through “taxation” and extortion, recruit new fighters, secure essential supplies, and expand territorial control. Witnesses said that they believed JNIM, whose fighters include many ethnic Fulani, attacked the site in retaliation for the military’s targeting of Fulani people since 2022. Fulani communities, they said, had also worked at the gold mining site but had been killed and otherwise abused by the military and VDPs who viewed them as JNIM collaborators. A 45-year-old man said that while hiding in a pit to avoid getting shot, he heard a fighter say: “You chased us away, but you won’t exploit this place.” At about 9:30 a.m. on September 5, an explosive weapon detonated as people rode a motorcycle along a dirt track about three kilometers from Mera village on the route to Soubo and Sissamba. It killed the 40-year-old driver and his two passengers, a 65-year-old woman and a 5-year-old boy. Mera is near the Soubo mining site, in an area where JNIM fighters frequently carry out attacks. Witnesses said they saw no JNIM fighters nearby at the time of the explosion but had seen at least four fighters traveling along the track on two motorbikes the previous evening. A motorbike rider, 40, said, “I saw a motorcycle in front of me with three people on it, and suddenly there was an explosion…. Dust flew around like a whirlwind. I heard a loud bang that threw me off [the bike]. The explosion shook the ground.” Human Rights Watch could not independently verify the type of explosive weapon used or how it was detonated. However, JNIM has repeatedly carried out attacks in Burkina Faso using IEDs. A 2025 report by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, a global coalition of nongovernmental organizations including Human Rights Watch dedicated to eradicating landmines and cluster munitions, noted JNIM’s use of IEDs in Burkina Faso. In 2024, Burkina Faso was among the countries with the highest rate of casualties—more than 200—due to landmines and explosive remnants of war globally. All parties to Burkina Faso’s armed conflict are bound by Common Article 3 to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, looting, and destroying civilian property. Individuals who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes. The Burkinabè government has an obligation to investigate and appropriately prosecute alleged war crimes committed within its territory. “JNIM forces should immediately cease unlawful attacks against civilians and appropriately punish responsible commanders,” Allegrozzi said. “Burkina Faso’s authorities should urgently improve demining efforts and increase assistance to victims of IED attacks.” Since the start of its insurgency in Burkina Faso in 2017, JNIM has repeatedly attacked civilians and forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people. Burkina Faso’s armed forces and VDPs have also committed serious abuses against civilians, especially Fulani, during operations against Islamist armed groups. In a report released in April 2026, Human Rights Watch documented that the Burkinabè and allied militia have targeted Fulani communities because of their alleged support for Islamist armed groups, resulting in the ethnic cleansing of entire communities. The nongovernmental group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data reported that JNIM carried out 125 attacks across Burkina Faso from January to August, resulting in the killing of 188 civilians, at least 16 of them in IED attacks. Explosive devices can be designed or fabricated to be detonated by a person’s presence, proximity, or contact. Such victim-activated devices function as antipersonnel mines and are prohibited internationally, regardless of whether assembled in a factory or improvised from locally available materials. They can also be made to detonate on command by various simple means or by a simple timer. Victim-activated IEDs are inherently indiscriminate weapons and are banned under the Mine Ban Treaty, which Burkina Faso ratified in 1998. Soubo, Yatenga Province, September 1 Witnesses said they identified the attackers by their clothes, including headscarves and a white flag with black writing, characteristic of JNIM. “They carried weapons and wore turbans,” said a 40-year-old artisanal miner and farmer. “They shouted Allah Akbar and shot at people at random.” JNIM is known to operate in the area and carry out attacks against government security forces and civilians. “The assailants began shooting everywhere and then went shed-by-shed,” a 37-year-old restaurant owner said. “I lay down in my restaurant and they found me.… They shot point-blank at two of my customers who fell in front of me.” She said that when JNIM fighters set her restaurant on fire, she had to get up to avoid being burned. One fighter wanted to kill her, but another told him to let her go because she was a woman. “They told me: ‘Tell your husbands not to come here anymore. These places belong to us.’” When residents who had fled the site of the attack returned, they found the victims’ bodies still on the ground or inside the mining pits. “I went back to the site three days later and saw the huge damage, a site covered in ashes,” said a 40-year-old artisanal miner. “I saw at least 20 bodies. The bodies were swollen and gave off a foul smell. I helped pick up the bodies and carry them for burial.” Residents said the bodies were buried in the cemeteries of the nearby villages of Soubo, Pirgo, and Sissamba. In June, Burkina Faso’s territorial administration minister had issued a decree suspending artisanal mining activities in Ouahigouya district from July 1 to September 30, to protect miners “from the high risk of landslides during the rainy season.” However, residents said, about a thousand people—mostly artisanal miners, but also shopkeepers, owners of small restaurants, and children—were at the site at the time of the attack. They said people had continued working despite the authorities’ suspension order, since officials never visited the site to enforce the suspension or check whether activities had ceased. “The terrorists burned a lot of property, huts under which there were small restaurants, motorcycles, small straw houses, mills, water pumps, and other equipment,” the 40-year-old artisanal miner said. “The fire spread from one hut to another. My barrel and my shed were also burned.” Human Rights Watch analyzed NASA satellite data and found evidence of numerous fires at the Soubo mining site on September 1 at 1:11 a.m. local time, corroborating witnesses’ accounts. Human Rights Watch also verified and geolocated four videos posted to TikTok on September 2 and 4, showing the destruction at the mining site. However, the videos only show a small part of the destruction visible in the satellite imagery. In imagery recorded on October 10, hundreds of structures are destroyed or no longer visible with burn scars on and around partially damaged structures, while others are completely destroyed. Satellite imagery recorded prior to the attack, on August 26, shows that the site contained at least 800 structures, consistent with witness accounts that at least 1,000 people were at the site. Click to expand Image Satellite imagery recorded on October 10, 2026 shows hundreds of structures destroyed or no longer visible at the Soubo gold mining site following the JNIM attack on September 1, 2026. Image © 2026 Planet Labs PBC. Analysis and Graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch. Human Rights Watch reviewed a list provided by residents with the names of 24 victims, all civilians, including three women, ages 31, 36, and 37, and 21 men, ages 27 to 45. Mera, September 5, Yatenga province A farmer, 43, working in a field with other men near the road said he rushed to the scene after hearing the explosion. “When we arrived, we found a large hole at least one meter deep,” he said. “A few pieces of the woman's remains were not far from the hole – the woman had no body left. The man had been propelled far from the hole, near the bushes, as well as the child who had lost his lower limbs.” “The blast knocked the wind out of me, dust filled my throat, and I couldn’t see anything,” a 37-year-old man said. “The debris went very high before falling everywhere. I smelled a sharp, irritating odor, like sulfur.” He said that he and other people “took plastic tarps, collected the bodies and body parts, and carried out the burial the same day just after 2 p.m. in Yaoua village.” Witnesses said that after the explosion, soldiers arrived at the scene. The farmer said, “The military stepped in after the explosion to secure the area, searched for other IEDs and defused three of them, so we could safely take the bodies and bury them.”

items.title: I would accept a government appointment if it’s not full-time – Fifi Kwetey
items.description: National Democratic Congress (NDC) General Secretary Fifi Fiavi Kwetey says he would accept a government appointment if it isn’t full-time. But he says holding no government position has been liberating as it lets him focus on the party and speak freely without worrying about reactions from the presidency or government. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, Mr Kwetey was asked whether he would have accepted an appointment if offered. “Why not? I wouldn’t have minded because as long as it’s not a full-time position,” he said. Mr Kwetey said he had not actively sought a government role. His priority was the party’s return to power and his responsibilities as General Secretary. “There are so many people who do not have any position. I have a position as a general secretary. It gives me liberty to be able to fully concentrate also on the party.” He said general secretaries had typically held government appointments, particularly as board chairs, across the two main political parties. That had not been his experience. “My national chairman has it. I don’t.” Mr Kwetey argued that combining the party role with a board chairmanship could create conflicting lines of authority. As General Secretary, he explained, he serves as the party’s chief executive and manages its interface with government. A board chairmanship would also place him under a minister. “But that minister actually is supposed to effectively be reporting to you as general secretary. So it’s a bit of a conundrum itself on its own, you know.” For him, not having a government appointment gives him room to address issues without worrying whether his comments will please those in power. “Is somebody happy in government? Is somebody happy at the presidency?” “It’s not my consideration. I do what I believe to be right for party, and it’s fine.” He also urged party members to work for the NDC’s strength out of conviction. “That we need to encourage a lot more people in the party to do what they do fundamentally because they want the party to be strong.”

items.title: Los demócratas arrasan en las ‘midterms’ a lomos del voto de castigo a la caótica presidencia de Trump

items.title: Los expertos de Trabajo recomiendan que el salario mínimo suba un 4,9% en 2027, hasta los 1.281 euros al mes
items.description: El equipo de expertos reunido por el Ministerio de Trabajo tiene ya lista su recomendación sobre la próxima subida del salario mínimo, la pieza clave que esperaba el Gobierno para aprobarla antes de que acabe la legislatura. Este grupo recomienda a Trabajo que suba el salario mínimo interprofesional (SMI) un 4,9% en 2027, de manera que crezca de los 1.221 euros brutos en 14 pagas que rigen este año a 1.281 euros. Es un salto mensual de 60 euros, en línea con la evolución interanual de los precios , según el texto elaborado por este grupo de académicos, sindicalistas y miembros del Ejecutivo y al que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS. Como en años anteriores con Yolanda Díaz como responsable de Trabajo, este informe es el paso previo a la negociación con sindicatos y patronales, donde se definirá cuánto sube exactamente el SMI. Las centrales piden un alza del 7% , los empresarios critican las “prisas” del ministerio y el Gobierno tiene claro que pretende elevar el suelo retributivo antes de las elecciones del 29 de noviembre. items.title: Scandal-hunting will keep NPP in opposition for a long time – Fifi Kwetey
items.description: NDC General Secretary Fifi Fiavi Kwetey has warned that the New Patriotic Party (NPP) risks a prolonged stay in opposition if it keeps hunting for scandals to revive its political fortunes. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he accused the NPP of manufacturing controversy around the evacuation of Ghanaians from South Africa. “You’re going to remain in this position for a long time unless you wake up and realise that Ghanaians have long passed this very low-level politicking.” His comments followed the NPP youth wing’s protest in Accra over the evacuation expenditure. Protesters demanded their money back and an account of an alleged GH¢16.4 million discrepancy. They also called for supporting payment records and an independent audit. Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has defended the GH¢49.72 million exercise, which covered 1,964 evacuees. He has rejected claims of unaccounted funds and requested a special audit by the Auditor-General. Mr Kwetey dismissed the NPP’s approach as political retaliation against Mr Ablakwa for exposing alleged wrongdoing under the previous government. “They come at you with every venom; they want to destroy at all costs.” The host challenged that position, citing disputed signatures, duplications and other discrepancies in the ministry’s documents. Mr Kwetey dismissed those concerns as peripheral and questioned whether the opposition had established any theft. “What have you been able to establish against the foreign Minister that is stolen? What? How much money? You can’t prove one.” He argued that scandal-hunting was a political practice he had resisted within his own party. Recalling the NDC’s move into opposition after the 2016 election, he said pressure to uncover scandals helped drive his decision to leave his position as ranking member for Trade and Industry. “One of the reasons why I quit the position as a ranking member was because I simply could not understand the expectation from my own corner that I must find scandal on NPP at all costs.” For him, scrutiny must follow genuine wrongdoing. “If there’s something genuinely wrong, I will speak. I’m not going to be fishing for scandal for the sake of it.” Mr Kwetey said the NPP had failed to learn from its 2024 electoral defeat. He argued that searching for scandals would not erase voters’ memories of its eight years in government. “It’s a total joke to go and do a demonstration; a demonstration on the back of what?” he asked.

items.title: How Texas Turned Blue
items.description: Photographs by Paola Chapdelaine For decades, Texas has been the foundation of the Republican Electoral College map, holding up the red bloc of midwestern and southern states like a pedestal. Democrats have long dreamed of winning it back, only for their hopes to be crushed in election after election. And now, suddenly, James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa have accomplished what no Democrat could for more than a generation: winning statewide elections in Texas. Whether or not Texas is truly a battleground state now, a few things have become clear. Republicans can no longer take Texas voters for granted. Donald Trump harmed his party’s chances by propping up a weak Senate candidate in Attorney General Ken Paxton. And even Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, couldn’t buy the result he wanted. Heading into election day, polls showed Talarico with a modest lead over Paxton, while the incumbent Republican governor, Greg Abbott, was favored to fend off Hinojosa. But not long after the polls closed, it became clear that both Talarico and Hinojosa would win comfortably. The Talarico Election Night party was jubilant, with cheers erupting every few minutes as new races were called for Democrats and updated results continued showing him with a sizable lead. James Edge, a Republican mayor pro tem from Bryan, Texas, stood eating a cookie and enjoying what he was seeing. He had endorsed Talarico just after Labor Day. “My party, the Republican Party, needed a kick in the pants,” he said. “This is uncharted waters. If it holds, it’s an earthquake like we’ve never seen.” [ Read: Trump has pushed some Texas Republicans too far ] At Paxton’s Election Night event in Dallas, party activists groaned as Fox News updated its ballot totals and the magnitude of the loss began to sink in. The Democrats even won the race for Texas railroad commissioner—a job held by Republicans for the past 36 years—as Jon Rosenthal easily defeated Bo French, who ran a race-baiting campaign that outraged the state’s growing Indian American population. Jarrod Atkinson, a Dallas-area Republican activist, walked out of the ballroom where Paxton was scheduled to speak, looking stunned. He laid the blame squarely on Trump. “The fact that he keeps telling everyone to vote like he’s on the ballot is absolutely insane,” he said. “He has said some of the dumbest things that have ever been uttered.” Before tonight, Texas had not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, and had not chosen a Democrat for the U.S. Senate since Lloyd Bentsen, in 1988. But the state’s shifting demographics have nurtured Democratic hopes of a comeback for years. Texas, which Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024, has grown significantly wealthier, more urban, and more racially diverse even as Republicans have dominated its politics. In fact, the shift traces in part to some of the very pro-business policies that have made Texas so appealing to large corporations. During the past three decades of GOP rule, the state has offered itself as a foil to New York and California, with cheaper housing, more job opportunities, lower taxes, and less red tape. The state’s population has grown more than 8 percent since 2020, absorbing more new residents than any other. More than 300 companies have relocated their corporate headquarters to Texas since 2015, including Tesla, Oracle, and Charles Schwab. Tech employment has been growing faster in Austin than in Silicon Valley. Republicans like to think of the influx as a political endorsement of GOP rule. But the newcomers are more racially diverse and more likely to be college-educated than the average Texan. Over the past decade, the percentage of adults in the state with a bachelor’s degree or higher—a group that has shifted decisively to the Democratic coalition—rose from 28 to 35 percent. Hispanics, who made up 40.9 percent of the population in 2025, are now a plurality of the state’s residents. Paola Chapdelaine for The Atlantic Supporters attend a rally at Stubb's Bar-B-Q in support of the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico. Demographic change alone was not enough to deliver a statewide election to Democrats. But Republicans entered this Senate race with at least two additional disadvantages. The first is broad discontent about the rising cost of living, which voters seem to have directed not just at Donald Trump but also at Texas’s ruling class. Republicans of yore had campaigned on the “Texas Miracle,” touting broad economic growth. That case became harder to make amid rising prices for groceries, gas, health care, and housing. “It felt like everything was on the upswing for a long time,” Nancy Zdunkewicz, an Austin-based Democratic pollster, told us. “The bill is now due.” [ Read: The GOP’s culture-war Hail Mary ] Mike Madrid, a political consultant who studies Hispanic-voting trends, told us that the percentage of early votes in the state included more ballots cast by Hispanic voters than any other group, including white voters. “That is something I have not seen in 35 years,” Madrid said. “If the economy were doing really well right now, we would not be seeing this.” In 2024, Hispanic Texans swung heavily toward Trump. This year, they appear to have shifted right back. Madrid argues that Hispanic voters are an emerging swing demographic, more populist than ideological, and that this year they’re mad about inflation. The lesson for Democrats, he said, is that the party needs a pro-growth message and a “new southern strategy” tailored to working-class Hispanic voters across the Sun Belt states, with Texas at the center. In the Senate race, Republicans compounded their disadvantages by nominating a deeply flawed candidate, while Democrats nominated one who positioned himself as the morally upstanding alternative. Paxton, whom Trump endorsed in the primary over the incumbent, John Cornyn, was known for a list of legal, ethical, and personal scandals far too extensive to summarize here. Dan Jackson, a truck driver and three-time Trump voter in Plano, said he “had some trouble” sorting out all the negative ads he’d seen this year. Ultimately, he voted for Abbott for governor—a safe choice, he reasoned—but went for Talarico for Senate because he doesn’t trust Paxton. “You’ve got, in Paxton, the worst statewide candidate to top the Republican ticket in the entire history of Republican hegemony in the state,” James Henson, the director of the Texas Politics Project at UT Austin, told us. “And then an unusually skilled Democratic candidate in Talarico, who came along at the right moment and has been able to execute better than any Democrat before him.” Paola Chapdelaine for The Atlantic Paola Chapdelaine for The Atlantic When Gina Hinojosa was considering whether to run for governor, she met with Beto O’Rourke, whose campaigns for Senate and governor had electrified a hopeful Democratic base only to end in disappointment on Election Day. Someone needed to run against Abbott, the entrenched and powerful incumbent, Hinojosa told him. Should she do it? One comment stood out: “Not one person can win Texas,” he told her, according to someone familiar with their conversation. “It has to be two.” O’Rourke told her that both times he was running statewide, he felt that his campaign would have benefited from a stronger ticket. The dynamic that emerged in 2026 was one in which Hinojosa and Talarico could work in tandem, sharing a similar message while energizing different pockets of the state. Talarico spoke openly about his faith, and had a sunny disposition that played well in rural areas. Hinojosa, a Latina woman, targeted the conservative suburban women known as MAGA moms who shared her concern about privatizing public schools. Talarico, in particular, ran as that rare political breed: a Democrat who seems genuinely comfortable talking about his Christian faith. He was willing to mix it up with Joe Rogan and Fox News hosts. He was careful not to mention Trump, lest he alienate the many Texans who had voted for the president but whose votes he would need. Talarico’s final rally, held in an outdoor amphitheater filled with nearly 2,000 people, was an anxiety-filled dose of optimism. “I’m a worrywart,” Pauline Bryson, an Austin resident attending the rally, said. “But a very hopeful worrywart.” Some recalled bawling when Beto O’Rourke lost in 2018; they questioned whether it was okay to be hopeful. But this time felt different—right? Right? Through a hoarse voice, Talarico asked the crowd to be the “slingshot” to help his David beat the Paxton Goliath. [ Read: Texans will decide if Jesus was a lefty ] Some 225 miles away, Paxton’s campaign sputtered to a close. Paxton’s team had planned to end his campaign with a rally at the Alamo Monday evening. They canceled the event with no explanation, and Paxton’s finale took place instead at Matt’s Rancho Martinez, a Tex-Mex restaurant next to a Quality Inn on the side of the expressway north of Dallas. About 150 supporters showed up, helping themselves to free nachos and margaritas, and the NRA handed out trucker caps and stickers. Paxton had spent the final stretch traveling the state on what he called the “Come and Take It” tour, speaking at restaurants and other relatively small venues. His slogan and the cannon imagery on the side of his tour bus were meant to channel the defenders of the Alamo, and the breakaway defiance that produced the state’s independence. But it sounded like he was inviting Democrats to take the Senate seat. Local Republican officials warmed up the crowd with warnings that the state was on the cusp of disaster. One praised Paxton for helping defeat “the Bush cartel,” a reference to the state’s pre-Trump Republican establishment. A lot of the red-meat rhetoric was over the top, with communism, Sharia law, and forced vegetarianism looming over the taco bar. “If Texas turns blue, it’s our children and grandchildren who will be enslaved with it,” State Senator Bob Hall told the crowd. The Turkish former NBA player and political stuntman Enes Kanter, who has changed his name to Enes Kanter Freedom and more recently declared himself a woman who wants to play in the WNBA, came out to introduce Paxton. He told the audience “close your eyes and think about your daughter being in the same locker room with biological males.” There were gasps. Frank DeSimone, a software developer and local Republican precinct official who attended the Paxton rally, told us the booming suburbs north of Dallas, where he lived, were facing “a paradox.” Rapid growth brings rapid change, he said, jeopardizing the same things that attracted so many transplants—safe neighborhoods, good schools—in the first place. It was up to Republicans to stand for a set of “Texas values” that would win suburban voters over. DeSimone said he wanted to help grow the party by defining that in a big-tent way. Did he think Texas will be an up-for-grabs purple state in ’28? “It already is,” he said. For all his weaknesses, Paxton entered the general election with a not-so-secret weapon. Elon Musk poured almost $200 million into the state, the bulk of it to boost Paxton’s Senate bid. Musk’s home base is in the state, and he has located many of his businesses in Texas, with all the tax breaks and political connections that flow from that. On Monday morning, we paid a visit to a corner of Bastrop, Texas, that has become so identified with Musk that locals call it “Elon Land.” His tunnel-digging business, the Boring Company, is here, along with SpaceX and Starlink. Those companies have made some residents rich. But even in Elon Land, we found signs that his political reach is limited. Paola Chapdelaine for The Atlantic The entrance of the Boring Company, located in “Elon Land,” in Bastrop, Texas. Sebastyon Champion, a 38-year-old senior project manager working on the SpaceX facility, wore a Carhartt hat and a silver cross as he finished a pulled-pork sandwich at the Boring Bodega, a combination of a market, a bar, and a hair salon. He is well paid, living in an apartment complex so new that most units haven’t yet been sold, but he also noted that he paid $100 to put three-quarters of a tank into his truck that morning. He’s a conservative voter—“We have a saying here: Don’t California my Texas”—but was turned off by Paxton and his history of corruption. “Ken Paxton should be in jail,” he said. “I wouldn’t piss on him if he was on fire.” He voted for Abbott, but when it came to the Senate race, he went for a third-party candidate. In fact, over the course of several hours, in conversations with more than a dozen Texans whose livelihood depends on Musk—and in a setting directly across from a mammoth manufacturing plant the tech mogul is constructing—we could find no one who was supporting the candidate he had spent so much money to prop up. The lingering question, which will be litigated in election cycles to come, is whether a generational political realignment is taking place in one of the nation’s largest states—or whether Democrats just got lucky this time. “People who win think it’s about them. It’s always about their opponent,” Bill Miller, a lobbyist in Austin with connections to both parties, told us. “People vote against people. That’s our culture now. If Democrats think it’s because they got all the issues, they don’t. It’s the issues that Republicans are carrying are turning people off.” That might be true—but in two years, the GOP will still be defined by an incumbent president who is currently the most unpopular in the history of polling. Texas will be worth 40 electoral votes in the next presidential election, and there are few plausible Republican roads to victory without it. The last time a Democratic presidential candidate won the state was Jimmy Carter in 1976. Heading into 2028, Texas Democrats won’t be able to stop themselves from dreaming big. Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed to this report.

items.title: ¿Apoyar a las víctimas? Sí, pero si no molesta aVox
items.description: Déjenme que les cuente brevemente dos historias de vida y muerte, en principio muy diferentes entre sí, o tal vez no tanto. Juzguen ustedes. La primera es la de Ramón Baglietto, vecino de Azkoitia (Gipuzkoa), dueño de una tienda de muebles y simpatizante de la UCD. El 13 de mayo de 1980, a las nueve de la noche, llamó a su esposa, Pilar Elías, y le dijo: “Voy para casa”. No llegó. En el camino, un terrorista de ETA llamado Kandido Azpiazu lo acribilló a balazos. No era la primera vez que el asesino se cruzaba con su víctima. Lo contó Pedro Mari Baglietto, uno de los hermanos del asesinado: “En 1962, Ramón estaba en la puerta del negocio familiar cuando observó a una señora que llevaba a un niño en brazos y a otro de la mano, que salió corriendo justo en el momento en que se acercaba un camión. La señora se lanzó tras el muchacho con la intención instintiva de protegerlo, y a Ramón apenas le dio tiempo de quitarle al niño que tenía en brazos y ver con horror cómo la madre y el otro hijo morían aplastados. Pues bien, el niño que quedó en sus brazos aquel día sería, 18 años después, uno de los miembros del comando que acabó con su vida. El presunto autor del tiro de gracia”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Algo que podemos aprender de la muerte de Jesús de Miguel
items.description: No me busquen entre quienes a estas horas, envueltos en el peor fragor de todos, el del dolor mezclado con la muchedumbre iracunda, maldicen al portero Jesús Owono y piden para él que no vuelva a jugar al fútbol o una condena por homicidio imprudente . Tampoco entre quienes despachan la jugada como lance del juego, por habitual que sea, y cargan la responsabilidad a la mala suerte. Pónganme entre los que animan al duelo por Jesús de Miguel y a la compasión por Owono, que bastante tiene, y prefieren que esta tragedia sirva para examinar ciertas entradas en el fútbol; que la muerte de Jesús de Miguel no sea en vano, que se erradiquen entradas bárbaras en un campo que en muchas ocasiones, no digo esta, se cometen con la excusa de que el balón pasaba por ahí. He visto entradas parecidas a la de Owono, muchas de ellas movidas por ese dicho tan celebrado entre defensas de la escuela de Vinnie Jones , que dice que o pasa el balón, o pasa el delantero. Y en el Tenerife-Andorra tiene pinta de que algo parecido pensó Owono cuando Jesús de Miguel podía marcar el gol del triunfo: saltó el portero rodilla arriba y brazos extendidos. Una entrada salvaje de roja hecha a saber con qué pulsaciones. Cuesta aceptar que un futbolista haga algo tan propio de un partido —ir a por un balón, llegar tarde, llevarse por delante al rival— y que el desenlace sea tan brutal y distinto. Como si el atropello del videojuego de repente se tornase real. Pero es que siempre es real, por más pantallas que haya entre nosotros y nuestros ídolos. Delante de la tele y en el estadio se exige velocidad, garra y contacto, y los espectadores muchas veces terminamos normalizando lo que, fuera del bar, nos haría llamar a la policía. Ahora hay una vida, la vida normal que todos conocemos, en la que hoy estaríamos debatiendo si la roja merecía tres partidos de sanción o cinco; y otra vida, la vida incomprensible, una vida que ocurre una entre un millón, en la que lloramos un cadáver y discutimos si un portero merece volver a jugar. Esta última es una vida cuya probabilidad se puede reducir a cero si muchos jugadores, en lances parecidos, consiguen pensar una décima antes en el rival que en el resultado. Incluso pensar en sí mismos: la posibilidad, ínfima pero real, de que la sanción sea el menor de sus problemas.

items.title: El viaje surrealista de las piernas de Dalí en una caja de cartón: una ventana al ADN de la creatividad humana
items.description: Una caja de cartón con media pierna derecha del pintor Salvador Dalí recorrió 700 kilómetros por España hace una década, desde su tumba en Figueres (Girona) hasta el laboratorio del genetista Antonio Alonso , en la localidad madrileña de Las Rozas. El paquete incluía además tres dientes, cuatro uñas y un mechón de pelo del artista. La escena parecía un óleo surrealista del propio Dalí, con su iconografía de cadáveres despedazados , pero se trataba de una prueba científica ordenada por un juzgado para averiguar si el pintor era el padre de Pilar Abel, una pitonisa que aseguraba ser su hija. Seguir leyendo

items.description: Nicole Kidman ha explicado a la edición británica de Vogue que en sus escapadas a Ibiza, disfruta de ir a alguna rave , es decir, a una fiesta de música electrónica de larga duración que se suele celebrar en algún lugar alternativo como una nave industrial. Muchos comprendieron entonces que no son solo sus dotes como actriz, sino la experiencia, las responsables de que bordara la comentada escena de Babygirl en la que lo da todo en la pista de baile. “ Cena a las 22.30, discoteca a la 1. Me pongo gafas. A veces me pongo una peluca para disimular, una peluca oscura, y entonces puedo bailar. Mientras esté rodeada de gente, o sea, voy con mi gente, estoy bien. Lo necesito”, detalló a la publicación. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Hugo Morenilla, director de cine con 16 años: “No hace falta tener 25 años para perseguir un sueño”
items.description: Es de Barcelona y cuenta 16 años. Hugo Morenilla lo tiene claro: “Quiero ser el director más joven en ganar un premio Óscar”. Conoce bien el mundo del cine. A los seis años empezó a actuar y a los 13 creó su propia productora. Hasta ahora ha dirigido 15 cortos, nueve películas, tres videoclips y una serie. Todo ello antes siquiera de cumplir la mayoría de edad. Su objetivo es superar el récord de precocidad de Damien Chazelle. El director de La La Land recibió en 2016 el Óscar a mejor dirección con 32 años. A Morenilla le quedan unos 17 años para intentar arrebatarle ese récord y convertirse en el cineasta más joven en conseguir la estatuilla. Seguir leyendo

Un grupo similar en España debería sumar más de 2,5 millones. ¿Ha llegado a España este fenómeno? Por partes. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Audio | La abogada de Koldo García advirtió a la fiscal de la “sorpresa” que se llevaría al saber que ‘Okdiario’ pagaba la defensa: “No tengo nada que ver con el PSOE”
items.description: La abogada Leticia de la Hoz advirtió en julio a la Fiscalía Anticorrupción de la gran “sorpresa” que se llevaría al saber quién costeó la defensa de Koldo García, antiguo asesor del exministro José Luis Ábalos, juzgado y condenado en el Tribunal Supremo. Durante su interrogatorio en la Audiencia Nacional por el caso Leire Díez y ante la insistencia del ministerio público para que respondiera quién le había pagado y si había una vinculación con el PSOE, la letrada negó que el partido socialista estuviese detrás, antes de acogerse al secreto profesional y avisar a la acusación de que no iba bien encaminada. “No tengo absolutamente nada que ver con el PSOE, y no ha pagado la defensa de Koldo respecto de mí”, repitió De la Hoz, que meses más tarde ha revelado (tras requerirlo ahora el juez instructor Santiago Pedraz) que la web ultraderechista Okdiario le abonó 242.000 euros por ese trabajo de defensa de Koldo García . items.title: Más presupuesto y freno a los campus privados: Las claves de la huelga universitaria en Madrid
items.description: Trabajadores y estudiantes de las seis universidades públicas de Madrid están llamados este miércoles y mañana jueves a una huelga en contra de los recortes del Gobierno autonómico de Isabel Díaz Ayuso. El paro es distinto de la protesta indefinida del profesorado no universitario de la región, que ya entra en su cuarta semana, y comenzó a fraguarse antes del final del curso pasado. Los convocantes aspiran a vaciar los campus para sumarse a varios actos de las protestas que han pintado de verde el centro de Madrid. Hace justo un año miles de docentes, personal de servicios y alumnos salieron a las calles de la capital para exigir la subida del presupuesto universitario. El acuerdo de financiación firmado en marzo por los rectores y la Consejería de Educación no ha puesto fin al conflicto. Estas son las claves de la nueva huelga. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El mayor casero de Madrid, la agencia de vivienda social de la Comunidad, acelera los desalojos mientras mantiene pisos vacíos durante años
items.description: El mayor casero de Madrid, la Agencia de la Vivienda Social, aprieta cada vez con más fuerza a los inquilinos que considera irregulares. Hasta el 30 de septiembre había desalojado a 255 familias, según datos oficiales a los que ha accedido EL PAÍS. Es la cifra más alta desde 2015 y refleja la política de mano dura contra la ocupación impulsada por la presidenta Isabel Díaz Ayuso. El objetivo declarado es recuperar viviendas para adjudicarlas a familias que esperan su turno y cumplen los requisitos. Sin embargo, esa estrategia convive con cientos de pisos vacíos y con denuncias vecinales sobre inmuebles que permanecen cerrados durante años, protegidos con puertas de acero. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los seis detenidos por Blocus en Cataluña: administradores o agitadores en redes, sin relación entre sí
items.description: Los Mossos d’Esquadra, y también el resto de cuerpos policiales, están aplicando lo que prometieron: una política de tolerancia cero contra todos aquellos que participaron en la agitación o coordinación de los saqueos en Barcelona el pasado 24 de octubre a través de plataformas de mensajería bajo el fenómeno Blocus. Hasta el momento, han detenido a seis jóvenes en Cataluña, cuatro de ellos menores de edad. Los jueces han decretado prisión sin fianza para dos adultos, de 21 y 18 años, y el internamiento en un centro de menores para uno de 17 años. El Govern exige a las plataformas digitales que faciliten el nombre de las personas que crearon los grupos de mensajería. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Jesús Owono, el portero que solo quería cuidar a su familia
items.description: A Jesús Lázaro Owono Ngua quienes lo conocen lo llaman Chus . La trayectoria vital del guardameta del Andorra, implicado el lunes en el choque brutal que ayer le costó la vida a los 30 años al delantero del Tenerife Jesús de Miguel, tiene los mismos ribetes que muchas de las historias de la emigración africana a Europa. Owono nació en 2001 en Bata, la ciudad más poblada de Guinea Ecuatorial, y ocho años después abandonó la excolonia española y se mudó al País Vasco con su familia en busca de una vida más próspera. Sus primeras palabras en euskera las pronunció en la ikastola Ibai, situada en el barrio de Ibaeta de San Sebastián. Hubo un día en el colegio que el portero habitual no pudo jugar por lesión, y él se colocó bajo los palos. Fue la primera vez que Chus, con un cuerpo de Action Man que ahora tiene una estatura de 1,83 metros, exhibió una agilidad extraordinaria para lanzarse a despejar la pelota como si en vez de piernas tuviera muelles. Seguir leyendo

items.title: España salva el consenso iberoamericano con una declaración final de mínimos
items.description: La profunda brecha ideológica que divide al mundo se ha colado también en la negociación de la declaración conjunta de la XXX Cumbre Iberoamericana, que se celebra este miércoles y jueves en Madrid. Finalmente España, anfitriona de esta edición, ha logrado salvar los muebles de una cumbre con más ausencias de las previstas, a la que han dado plantón los principales mandatarios progresistas, como la mexicana Claudia Sheinbaum o el brasileño Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Pese a ello, los negociadores alcanzaron este martes un principio de acuerdo en torno a un texto de mínimos que debe ser ratificado por los jefes de las delegaciones de los 22 países de lengua española o portuguesa de Europa y América. No es un logro menor, ya que la anterior cumbre, celebrada en Cuenca (Ecuador), se cerró por primera vez en 33 años sin una declaración final. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Why Republicans Lost So Big
items.description: The president’s party is always expected to do poorly in midterm elections, just not this poorly. The results arriving tonight are a disaster for Donald Trump—the kind of complete repudiation that the president’s opponents have spent a decade pining for, but never quite achieving. On current trends, Democrats are not just poised to claim a large majority in the House of Representatives. They are also on track to capture the Senate by winning seats they hoped for, as in Texas, and others that they had no business hoping for, as in South Carolina. The rebuke looks too ubiquitous to be confined to the gripes of any particular subset of voters. In Miami-Dade County, in Florida, for example, the impressive Latino support that Trump built up in his 2024 win appears to have totally evaporated . Kansas is on the verge of electing a Democratic senator—for the first time in a century. Democrats in Ohio seem likely to flip both the governor’s mansion and a U.S. Senate seat. Earlier today, a (Never Trump) Republican operative in the Midwest texted me, saying, “Our party badly needs an acid lava barbed-wire enema and I’m hoping we get it tonight.” Voters heard this wish. How did the GOP’s situation get so bad? A moralizing account might say that Trump is getting just deserts for his precedent-breaking behavior in office—the great personal enrichment, the weaponization of the justice system against his enemies, the dismantling of agencies without congressional consent. But this assumes too much about the propriety of American voters—who, after all, returned the president to office after he had tried to overturn his election loss in 2020. The more obvious explanation for Republicans’ poor performance is economic. Having come to office by exploiting discontent with inflation under Joe Biden, Trump seemed to think that the same rules would not apply to him while in office. The president has launched trade wars against the rest of the world, increasing the costs of imported goods, in addition to passing a massive tax cut and encouraging the AI-spending boom, which have pushed up interest rates. Most disastrously, he launched a war of choice against Iran that has raised the cost of gas and diesel. [ Read: The beginning of the end for Trump ] Only 38 percent of Americans now say that they approve of the president’s job performance. Trump and his allies attempted to juice their odds of holding the House by having Republican-led states aggressively gerrymander their districts. This strategy did not work. Unlike the president, Democrats learned the lessons of the last election: both that incumbents were vulnerable to attacks over the cost of living and that they had veered too far to the left on immigration and social-justice issues such as trans rights. The party has many sects—urban socialists, rural populists, “abundance”-pilled technocrats—that converged on a common message: the issue of “affordability,” on which Republicans were weak. All of these factions can be expected to jockey for credit in the party’s election victory, but Democrats’ all-terrain overperformance suggests that it was Republican actions in leadership that lost the election. The president’s predilection for underwhelming candidates, including the scandal-ridden Ken Paxton as Senate nominee in Texas and the underqualified Darline Graham in South Carolina, was a factor. But most of the problem seems to have been the president’s own policy making—a drag so serious that it imperiled experienced and established Republicans such as Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Governor Greg Abbott of Texas. The imminent demise of Trumpism has been predicted many times in the past decade. Even now, it cannot be guaranteed. The repudiation of Trumpism at the ballot box does not spell its demise even in the Republican Party. Such is the president’s hold among his loyal base. Democrats will be able to stymie the White House with budget battles and constant investigations, and will likely be in a position to block any Supreme Court nominees. Tonight’s outcome does not so much foretell a powerless president as it does an angry and perhaps even more disinhibited one. All of the president’s signature policy decisions of this term—the Iran war, the trade wars, special military operations in Venezuela and the Caribbean Sea—were launched without any congressional input whatsoever. Although Congress will more jealously try to guard its power under Democratic control, the imperial presidency is well entrenched. Trump’s power will eventually end—but only after one more election.

items.title: Oil edges down as investors await US midterm election results
items.description: Oil prices slipped in early trade on Wednesday as investors awaited US midterm election results and their potential impact on Middle East peace talks, even after industry data showed US crude stocks unexpectedly fell last week. Brent futures fell 26 cents, or 0.25%, to $103.34 a barrel by 0157 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 53 cents, or 0.55%, to $95.56. In the previous session, Brent eased more than 1% ​to its lowest level in nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to ​end the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Vote counting was underway in the ⁠US midterm elections , which will determine whether Trump’s Republican Party retains control of Congress for ​the rest of his second term. Markets remained on watch for any progress in talks to ​end the US-Israeli war with Iran, as Qatar stepped up mediation efforts to avert an escalation of attacks after the US midterm elections. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday that Iran and the ​United States remain far from a deal to end their war. The United States carried out “defensive” ​strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said on ‌Tuesday. Another ⁠official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations. US President Donald Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that the United States had no immediate plans to strike Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” Trump said ​in the six-minute telephone ​interview. Meanwhile, crude stocks fell ⁠by 5.27 million barrels in the week ended October 30, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Eight analysts polled ​by Reuters had expected, on average, a rise of about 880,000 ​barrels in ⁠crude inventories. Gasoline stocks rose by 1.43 million barrels, while distillate inventories fell by 1.19 million barrels from a week earlier, the sources said. “Diesel inventories remain tight, while gasoline stocks rose more ⁠than ​expected. The data are broadly supportive of oil prices,” ​Haitong Futures said in a note on Wednesday. Official data from the US Energy Information Administration is due at 10:30 ​a.m. EST (1530 GMT) on Wednesday.
