items.title: Microsoft brevète une IA capable de modifier les paroles et les mouvements des lèvres en direct
items.description: Microsoft a déposé un brevet décrivant une technologie d’intelligence artificielle capable de modifier les propos d’une personne filmée en direct, tout en adaptant les mouvements de ses lèvres au nouveau discours. Une innovation qui pourrait faciliter la traduction et le nettoyage audio, mais qui soulève également des questions sur l’authenticité des images et la désinformation. Baptisé « amélioration des flux vidéo grâce à l’IA » , le dispositif décrit dans ce brevet permettrait de transformer une séquence audiovisuelle avec un délai estimé entre une et dix secondes. L’intelligence artificielle interviendrait à la fois sur la piste sonore et sur l’image, en modifiant les mouvements des lèvres afin de rendre les changements quasiment imperceptibles. Parmi les applications envisagées figure le nettoyage des prises de parole. Le système pourrait notamment supprimer les hésitations, comme les « euh », corriger certains mots mal prononcés, filtrer les vulgarités ou encore atténuer les bruits de fond. Les modifications pourraient être personnalisées selon différents paramètres, notamment l’âge, les langues parlées ou le lieu de résidence de l’utilisateur. Le logiciel pourrait également intervenir sur les expressions familières et les mots inventés, afin d'adapter le discours aux préférences de la personne qui regarde la vidéo. Autre possibilité : la traduction en temps réel. Lorsqu’un intervenant s’exprime dans une langue étrangère, l’IA pourrait remplacer ses paroles par leur traduction et ajuster simultanément les mouvements de ses lèvres pour synchroniser l’image avec le nouvel audio. Une perspective qui pourrait bouleverser les métiers de la traduction et du doublage. À l’heure où les deepfakes et les contenus générés par IA alimentent les inquiétudes autour de la désinformation, la possibilité de transformer les propos d’une personne pendant une diffusion en direct pourrait fragiliser la confiance du public. Un spectateur pourrait ainsi entendre une version modifiée d’un discours sans nécessairement savoir que les paroles originales ont été remplacées. Le brevet prévoit toutefois la conservation d’une version de référence, non modifiée, du flux vidéo. Le dispositif pourrait fonctionner sur différents supports, notamment les smartphones, les tablettes, les caméras ou les lunettes connectées. Il convient néanmoins de rappeler qu’un brevet ne signifie pas qu’un produit sera commercialisé. Microsoft n’a, à ce stade, annoncé aucun déploiement de cette technologie. Le document ne précise pas non plus comment les utilisateurs pourraient identifier les séquences modifiées. The post Microsoft brevète une IA capable de modifier les paroles et les mouvements des lèvres en direct appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Bigwigs review KP situation after federal takeover
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and its main ally, the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), on Tuesday held a meeting to review the situation in Khyber Pakh­tunkhwa (KP) following the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule, and discussed the proposed Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Reforms (PCER). The consultative meeting was convened by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and attended by PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari and his delegation, comprising Senate Chairman Yousuf Raza Gilani, Senator Sherry Rehman and Raja Pervez Ashraf. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti. Some federal cabinet members and senior officials also attended the meeting. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Shehbaz also held a separate meeting with Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) Field Marshal Asim Munir to discuss the overall situation in the country, a source in the Prime Minister’s Office told Dawn . When contacted, a source privy to the meeting said it was a long-overdue meeting with the prime minister, during which the situation in all provinces was discussed. KP Governor Faisal Karim Ku­ndi briefed the PM on the latest situation in the province, particularly administrative measures and the issue of terrorism. Similarly, Balochistan Governor Sarfraz Bugti apprised the meeting of the security situation in his province. The source said the proposed formation of the Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Reforms also came under discussion, with the prime minister expressing the desire that the committee be constituted without further delay. The source said Mr Bilawal informed the prime minister that his party would soon submit the names of its nominees to National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq for the parliamentary committee. Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

items.title: Tesla misled South Korean customers about automated-driving tech, consumer group alleges
items.description: Tesla has misled tens of thousands ​of South Korean customers by marketing driver-assistance software that the company knows cannot be legally used in most of its vehicles in the country, according ‌to a complaint an advocacy group plans to file with a consumer protection agency on Thursday. Tesla has marketed Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software to prospective buyers in South Korea for years, often collecting lump-sum payments of 9.043 million won ($6,726). FSD can be used on about 20% of Tesla vehicles registered in South Korea — those manufactured in the US, Tesla Korea country manager Seo Young-deuk said in parliamentary testimony last month. Those cars meet US ​vehicle-safety standards that South Korea recognises as part of a free trade agreement, according to the forthcoming complaint to the Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC), seen by Reuters. The ​complaint to the regulator, which also handles antitrust, has not been previously reported. Most Tesla vehicles in South Korea, however, are manufactured in China, ⁠where no such agreement exists. Tesla only recently started the process for obtaining FSD certification for China-made vehicles, despite charging customers for the software for more than three years. Tesla did ​not respond to requests for comment. A KFTC official said the agency launched a probe earlier this year into Tesla’s advertising of its FSD system and has received written responses from ​the company, but declined to provide further details. SOUTH KOREAN FAIR TRADE COMMISSION INVESTIGATING It is unclear how many South Korean customers purchased FSD subscriptions on ineligible vehicles, but Tesla has sold more than 170,000 Shanghai-produced vehicles in South Korea since 2023, according to Tesla data sent to South Korea’s National Assembly. “Tesla generated substantial revenue by selling an expensive driver-assistance system to mass-market buyers who cannot use it for even a single day,” ​said Choi Young-suk, who leads automotive issues at the advocacy group Citizens United for Consumer Sovereignty. Tesla continued to market FSD as sales of ineligible China-manufactured Teslas surged in South Korea ​in recent years. Sales of FSD-incompatible Teslas made in China grew more than fivefold in South Korea from 2023 through last year, when 99% of new Teslas sold in South Korea could not legally ‌use FSD, ⁠according to data Tesla submitted to the National Assembly. Despite years of promises from CEO Elon Musk that all Teslas would soon become fully driverless vehicles, FSD is not autonomous and requires active human supervision. Tesla has sought to expand FSD’s reach beyond North America, particularly in Europe, where the company has waged a pressure campaign against European regulators. TESLA SALES SURGE IN SOUTH KOREA Tesla surpassed BMW this year as South Korea’s top imported-car brand, according to South Korean import data. Tesla sold FSD for one-time payments for years before the service activated last year, then shifted to a monthly subscription of 150,000 won ($112) in August. The complaint alleges that Tesla promoted FSD ⁠last year as “coming soon” and posted a demonstration video filmed in South Korea without clearly disclosing that the technology could only be used in a small fraction of Teslas being sold. Tesla knew those limitations but continued to market the software to all customers, the complaint said. Tesla ​Korea manager Seo testified during an October 8 parliamentary hearing that the company had not formally requested FSD testing from the transport ​ministry. Two weeks later, ⁠Tesla applied for certification. The ministry said FSD does not comply with local safety rules, including requirements that drivers keep their hands on the wheel, according to a statement it sent to a lawmaker that Reuters reviewed. The transport ministry could not be reached for comment. The consumer group accused Tesla Korea of deceptive marketing and asked the KFTC to issue a temporary cease-and-desist order on marketing FSD for ineligible vehicles, impose administrative fines, and refer the case to state investigators. A Seoul court last month dismissed a lawsuit filed by Tesla owners seeking refunds for its FSD option, which Tesla did not activate in South Korea until late last year. The court rejected their claim that Tesla failed to deliver the driver-assistance system, saying regulatory and legal ​restrictions limited the company’s ability to roll out additional functions.

items.title: Independent auditor to scrutinise Auditor-General’s accounts
items.description: Parliament has taken steps to subject the financial records of the Auditor-General’s Office to independent scrutiny after approving a committee report recommending the appointment of an external auditor to examine its accounts. The House adopted the report of an Ad Hoc Committee on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, during its first sitting following a recess. The recommendation seeks to give effect to Article 187 of the 1992 Constitution, which requires Parliament to appoint an auditor to examine and report on the accounts of the Office of the Auditor-General. The constitutional provision states: “The accounts of the office of the Auditor-General shall be audited and reported upon by an auditor appointed by Parliament.” The proposed arrangement is intended to ensure that the financial operations of the institution responsible for auditing public accounts are themselves subjected to an independent audit process. The Auditor-General’s Office plays a central role in promoting financial accountability in the public sector through the examination of government accounts and the reporting of irregularities and weaknesses in public financial management. The appointment of an external auditor is therefore expected to reinforce the oversight framework governing the institution and provide an additional layer of accountability. No individual has been named for the assignment following the adoption of the report. Parliament is expected to take the necessary steps to select an auditor in accordance with the constitutional requirement. The move also brings into focus the constitutional principle that public institutions, including those entrusted with scrutinising the use of public funds, must themselves be subject to appropriate checks and balances.

items.title: NPP targeting Ablakwa for exposing wrongdoing under Akufo-Addo – Fifi Kwetey
items.description: NDC General Secretary Fifi Fiavi Kwetey has accused the New Patriotic Party (NPP) of targeting Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa for exposing alleged wrongdoing under its administration. Speaking on JoyNews’ PM Express on Tuesday, November 3, he challenged the opposition party to produce evidence that the minister had stolen public funds. Kwetey dismissed the campaign against Ablakwa as retaliation for his role in holding the NPP to account while it was in government. “They come at you with every venom; they want to destroy at all costs.” Asked whether Ablakwa was being targeted for his previous actions, he replied, “Of course, it’s targeted.” His comments followed the NPP youth wing’s demonstration in Accra over spending on the evacuation of Ghanaians from South Africa. Protesters demanded the recovery of money they allege was unaccounted for. The party has questioned an alleged GH¢16.4 million discrepancy involving the evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians. It is demanding flight invoices, payment records, a full beneficiary list and an independent audit. During the interview, the host raised concerns about signatures and alleged duplications in documents released by the ministries. Kwetey dismissed those concerns as peripheral. He argued that Ablakwa’s previous disclosures involved evidence of alleged theft and abuse. “He was providing evidence, hardcore evidence, of stealing that was going on, of abuse that was going on, providing authentic documentation.” Kwetey also questioned complaints about payments raised months after recipients allegedly collected their money. He maintained that they should have reported any shortfall at the airport. He accused the NPP of searching for a scandal without establishing theft. “What have you been able to establish against the foreign Minister that is stolen? What? How much money? You can’t prove one.” Kwetey said his opposition to manufacturing scandals extended to his own party. Recalling his time as the ranking member for Trade and Industry after the NDC’s 2016 election defeat, he said pressure to find scandals had contributed to his decision to leave the role. “If there’s something genuinely wrong, I will speak. I’m not going to be fishing for scandal for the sake of it.” He warned that the NPP would struggle to recover politically if it continued on its current path. “You’re going to remain in this position for a long time unless you wake up and realise that Ghanaians have long passed this very low-level politicking.”

items.title: Fifi Kwetey challenges NPP to prove Foreign Affairs Minister stole evacuation funds
items.description: NDC General Secretary Fifi Fiavi Kwetey has challenged the New Patriotic Party (NPP) to prove that Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa stole money meant for evacuating Ghanaians from South Africa. Speaking on JoyNews’ PM Express on Tuesday, November 3, he dismissed the opposition party’s protest over the expenditure as politically motivated. “What have you been able to establish against the foreign Minister that is stolen? What? How much money? You can’t prove one.” His challenge followed an NPP youth demonstration in Accra demanding accountability over the evacuation. Protesters demanded their money back and explanations for an alleged GH¢16.4 million discrepancy. They also sought flight invoices, payment records and an independent audit. The dispute concerns a reported GH¢49.72 million operation to evacuate 1,964 Ghanaians following xenophobic violence and intimidation in South Africa. The Minority has questioned beneficiary registers, duplicate entries and other expenditure records. Those allegations do not establish that money was stolen. Mr Kwetey maintained that the NPP was searching for a scandal against a minister who had exposed wrongdoing under its administration. “They come at you with every venom; they want to destroy at all costs.” When the host raised concerns about signatures and duplications in the ministry’s documents, Mr Kwetey dismissed them as peripheral. He argued that Mr Ablakwa’s previous allegations against the NPP had been supported by substantive evidence. “He was providing evidence, hardcore evidence, of stealing that was going on, of abuse that was going on, providing authentic documentation.” Mr Kwetey also questioned complaints about evacuation support payments raised months after beneficiaries returned. He argued that recipients should have reported any shortfall at the airport or soon afterwards. Turning to the demonstration, he challenged its basis. “It’s a total joke to go and do a demonstration, a demonstration on the back of what.” He said his objection to manufacturing scandals extended to his own party. Recalling his time as an opposition MP after the 2016 election, he said pressure to find wrongdoing at all costs had contributed to his decision to leave his ranking role on Parliament’s Trade and Industry Committee. “If there’s something genuinely wrong with NPP, I will speak.” He accused the opposition of relying on scandal hunting instead of learning from its 2024 electoral defeat, adding, “How desperate can you be, NPP?”

items.title: New provinces, old solutions
items.description: MANY years ago, a senior official of a multilateral development bank delivered a harsh indictment of Pakistan’s state of affairs: it is a seriously large country run by a succession of non-serious policymaking elite. While the setting for the delivery of this critique was an informal one, it left one pondering its accuracy. Sadly, Pakistan’s ruling elites, irrespective of the political flag they bear, regularly try and prove the gentleman right. The recent spate of political statements on the creation of new provinces serves as an example. Administrative boundaries are not sacrosanct and must be viewed as mechanisms designed to serve evolving and defined public interest. Speaking about the creation of new provinces is not, therefore, tantamount to a conspiracy. Rather it reflects a healthy approach to reassessing their utility and viability. That said, restructuring a federation is not a trifling matter as its implications run deep and wide — from the obvious fiscal imperatives and changes to the balance of political representation, to the everyday impact on public service delivery and on the lives of citizens. Hasty, discordant political sound bites cannot, therefore, be a substitute for rigorous, extensive, and inclusive deliberation and analysis. The experience of other nations in this respect, including several where the author has had the privilege of leading the process, is instructive. There are two common strands of note. First, there is no single model to follow and changes are rooted in legal, political, and economic contexts. Second, political motives aside, each effort identified specific problems that the change was intended to solve. India’s establishment of Telangana was characterised by strong institutional arrangements, and extensive public engagement over an 11-month period. Brazil’s division of Goiás to form Tocantins responded to a long-standing public movement and leveraged constitutionally mandated plebiscitary mechanisms for public consent. In Russia, consolidation rather than fragmentation served as the principle for establishing the Zabaykalsky Krai region, with improved living standards being a clearly defined objective. Accelerating socioeconomic development was also the raison d’être for Timor-Leste’s establishment of the world’s newest Special Administrative Region in Oé-Cusse. From these and other global experiences, one can distill several insights and lessons for Pakistan. Lesson 1: Never treat the issue of creating new regions as merely redrawing the map. This reductive approach will upend any potential benefits that might accrue from a careful and considered process of reviewing how government is structured. The era of arbitrary, extractive cartography — for example, the Radcliffe Line, the Sykes-Picot Agreement, and Cecil Rhodes’s British South Africa Company — is dead and should stay that way. Pakistan should frame the issue of new provinces not as a form of territorial re-engineering but as a fundamental state reform aimed at reducing inequality, democratising economic and developmental opportunities, and improving public services. Lesson 2: Defined public interest, as opposed to political ambition or the facilitation of vested interests, should be the principal driver for change. Deep and genuine engagement with the public, not just their representatives, must constitute the starting point, not the finish line, and be non-negotiable. Furthermore, a distinction must be made between public need — the genuine reasons which justify change — and public demand — which can be easily manufactured through weaponising algorithms and orchestrated street power. The stronger the mechanisms for filtering out political noise and faux narratives, the greater the likelihood of neutralising proxy gerrymandering on public opinion. Administrative boundaries are not sacrosanct and must be viewed as mechanisms designed to serve evolving and defined public interest. Lesson 3:There needs to be absolute clarity on the purpose of the proposed changes, an agreement on the precise problems the changes set out to resolve, and complete transparency on plans. Vague, stylised assertions around improving governance and service delivery, and absence of transparency on both purpose and process, will only serve as a petridish for political and social discontent and extended, simmering disputes. Three other insights, peculiar to Pakistan’s context are important to highlight: first, the functionalisation and empowerment of local governments must be embedded within the debate on new provinces, as these are not mutually exclusive discussions. Second, it is necessary to look under the hood of how provinces themselves create administrative units, based as they are on administrative fiat rather than legislative approval — otherwise, we risk repeating the mistake made under the 18th Amendment’s Article 140-A, which left it to the provinces to establish independent local governments (they didn’t). Third, rejigging old solutions wrapped inside tired narratives and tactics (administrative fiat, holding illegal/ mala fide referendums, relying heavily on ethno-linguistic nationalism as a criterion) will be unfortunate. To move forward, a three-step roadmap is proposed: 1: Establish a ‘Commission for Citizen-Centric Change’ as a multi-stakeholder, cross-party, independent, and empowered institutional arrangement to lead the process. As part of its work, it should be tasked with extensive public engagement, and the conduct of technical analysis to determine criteria, weigh options, and ensure transparency and knowledge management. 2: Institute a three-dimensional ‘Public Interest Test’ framework that includes an assessment of the public benefits and whether they meet citizen aspirations and socioeconomic needs; a fiscal viability review to determine financial and economic sustainability; and an institutional readiness mapping to measure state capabilities and agility. 3: Test this framework and institutional arran­gements by targeting one province. Punjab is the most obvious case for review given its size and the ongoing debate on a south Punjab province. It should be used as a policy lab. Results emerging from this lab should inform a nationwide scaling.Indeed, it is time to get serious. The writer is a former adviser to the chair of the G77 and China. Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

I said no, I’m not doing it. That’s me. If there’s something genuinely wrong with NPP, I will speak.” He said the pressure extended beyond finding fault to creating scandals where none existed. “But in this situation, I must find scandal at all costs. If there is none, I must manufacture one.” Mr Kwetey drew on that experience to criticise the NPP’s campaign against Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa over the evacuation of Ghanaians from South Africa. The NPP youth wing demonstrated in Accra on Tuesday, demanding accountability over an alleged GH¢16.4 million discrepancy in evacuation expenditure. Protesters demanded their money back, along with flight invoices, beneficiary records, and an independent audit. The dispute concerns spending on the evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians. The Minority has questioned payment records and alleged that some beneficiaries received less than they were entitled to. Mr Ablakwa has denied wrongdoing and invited an Auditor-General’s audit. During the interview, the host challenged Mr Kwetey over concerns about signatures and duplicate entries in the ministry’s documents. Mr Kwetey dismissed those issues as peripheral. He argued that Mr Ablakwa was being targeted because of his role in exposing alleged wrongdoing under the previous government. He challenged the NPP to prove that the minister stole public funds. “What have you been able to establish against the Foreign Minister that was stolen? What? How much money? You can’t prove one.”

items.title: Repudiation
items.description: P resident Trump has been the dominant political figure of this century. He pulled off one of the most unlikely campaign victories in American history, and then staged the greatest political comeback. He has altered the United States’ relationship with the world, rewritten the rules and expectations of the presidency, inflamed the nation’s divisions, and changed how—and how often—Americans think about his office. He is omnipresent, and draws his power from that ubiquity. But tonight, Trump has been forced to face his political mortality. He asked voters to make these midterm elections a referendum on him, to imagine that his name was on the ballot. They listened—and then rejected him. It is a stunning, widespread rebuke. Democrats appear poised to win the House and, if trends hold, could also capture the Senate after Americans registered their strong disapproval of the direction in which the president has taken the country over the past two years. Trump will now likely have to deal with congressional Democrats who could block his agenda and wield the power of the subpoena. He also must face the possibility that the political party he remade in his image may soon start looking beyond him. Donald J. Trump is now officially, thoroughly a lame duck. But we haven’t heard the last of him. He remains the commander in chief, dominates global affairs, wields the expansive power of executive orders, and remains unequaled at capturing attention. He has escaped the political graveyard more than once before, and emerged stronger. Yet for all his power, for all his volume, he cannot browbeat the unrelenting calendar: The next national election will be the one to replace him. Trump will before long begin to slip in the headlines, pushed off the front page by the presidential campaign. He’ll face the possibility of being succeeded by a Democratic president who could employ the Department of Justice to plumb the previous four years and look into Trump’s allies, friends, family, and businesses. And he’ll confront arguably his greatest fear: irrelevance. Trump will not go quietly. It is not clear whether he and fellow Republicans will even accept the midterm results—and he has defied expectations so often that it would be a foolish exercise to set any. Tonight’s expected losses will not humble him. But they mark the beginning of the end. T rump’s midterm campaign ended in the most ridiculous, yet predictable, way possible. For months, the president had been accused of being out of touch, of losing his once-unmatched feel for what animated his supporters. He has mocked affordability concerns while his own fortune has swelled, started a war that Americans did not want, remodeled the White House, and planned various monuments to himself. And then yesterday, he decided that the best way to push back against the accusation that he’d been consumed with vanity projects and corrupt bargains would be to deliver the final speech of the campaign cycle at the site of his most absurd, failed renovation project. To the dismay of Republicans everywhere, Trump stood in front of the Reflecting Pool on the eve of Election Day and delivered a defense of a project that was doomed by algae and the shoddy work of a no-bid contractor. The project—which Trump had falsely claimed was derailed by vandalism—ran millions of dollars over budget and surely earned not a single vote in places such as Michigan, Kansas, and Alaska. Worst of all, the detour to revisit the Reflecting Pool distracted from Trump’s true closing message: that Senator Jon Husted of Ohio has a great body. [ Read: Trump is closing from behind ] Trump was a late entrant on the campaign trail, and had to be talked into holding rallies over the past month or so. But once he was, he insisted that the election be about himself and his successes, and make no acknowledgment of any missteps or empathy for those who are struggling. He insisted that many campaign ads feature him. He demanded a first-of-its-kind midterm political convention, though few who attended the festivities in Dallas seemed happy to be there. Trump threw himself into the campaign, holding nearly-two-hour rallies night after night across the country. But these road shows weren’t quite the same as those that became the defining political event of the past decade. They were smaller than normal, and few were outdoors (in part because of security concerns). One rally in Ohio in the campaign’s final fortnight was held in a small gym, and others featured plenty of empty seats. More striking was where the rallies were held: nearly half in deep-red states where Trump has easily won in the past and has rarely needed to campaign. That led to bigger, more enthusiastic crowds—people in a place like Corinth, Mississippi, were more excited to see Trump for the first time than, say, those in Grand Rapids, Michigan, where he has held more than half a dozen rallies over the years. But the geography also told a story: Trump had to visit Republican strongholds such as South Carolina and Montana because seats in those states were suddenly in play and his faithful had to be summoned. But once there, what did Trump really have to offer? Voters, per polling, are angry over his string of broken promises, including his vows to bring down prices, not start new wars, release the Epstein files, and deport only the “worst of the worst.” The parties of incumbent presidents traditionally fare poorly in the midterms, but Trump is also underwater on several of what used to be his strongest issues, such as the economy and immigration. He forced out multiple incumbent senators for being disloyal and backed some problematic candidates, all of which put more races into play. He gave Republican candidates very little to run on, as voters furiously reacted to an economy that seemed to benefit only the rich (a category that includes the president’s family and Cabinet). Instead, Trump tried to recycle culture-war issues from campaigns past, including fears about transgender surgeries, Muslim terrorists, and even communism. [ Read: Going hungry in Trump’s economy ] He seemed out of step not just with the public but, in many cases, with his own party. Despite warnings that AI could wipe out humanity (or at least a lot of jobs), Trump backed the nascent technology and its data centers—even as the public turned on them—because tech companies are propping up the stock market. He supported a controversial attack ad in the Ohio governor’s race that the state’s Republican governor denounced. He sided with Russia in its war with Ukraine. He threatened to once more bomb Iran. And there really was a lot of talk about butts, which will surely confuse future historians. Americans didn’t seem to go for it. As of this writing Democrats were well on track to decisively take the House. But the story is the Senate: Democrats have already flipped North and South Carolina and easily held on to Georgia. Ohio, Texas, and other deep-red strongholds may soon join them. As those results came in, Trump took to social media to duck blame—and contradict the central message of his campaign, writing, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” T rump is now in a new place , and one he won’t like. In his first midterm election, in 2018, Democrats gained control of the House, but that victory was offset by GOP wins in the Senate. House Democrats slowed the president’s agenda, but their 2019 impeachment effort over Ukraine only bolstered Trump’s approval ratings—and he still felt bullish about his reelection chances on the back of a strong economy. (Then, of course, came the pandemic.) Many Democrats say they’ve learned their lesson. Senior members in the party, including Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next House speaker, have been cagey as to their plans for power. The Democratic Party’s approval ratings remain low, and although not being a Republican boosted many Democrats in this year’s campaign, that won’t be the case going forward. Jeffries has signaled that he will focus on measures to try to address affordability and health-care challenges. Democrats are going to say “no” a lot, and now that it appears that they will capture the Senate too, they will likely make it difficult for Trump to confirm any of his nominees, including possible Supreme Court justices. But the Democratic Party’s base is hungry to hold the Trump administration accountable: for DOGE’s destruction of the government, for war, for foreign business deals masquerading as diplomacy, for profiting off the presidency. Accusations of corruption against Trump and his administration have proliferated compared with in his first term. Democrats have promised to issue subpoenas and parade administration officials through the Capitol’s hearing rooms—if they agree to show up. Some close to Trump have theorized that he doesn’t mind having a foil in Washington, and that he would be comfortable tangling with congressional Democrats again. “He likes to have someone to fight—and someone to blame,” one close outside adviser told me on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal dynamics. But Trump is leery about some of the possible investigations and does not want to be impeached again. (Democrats might be more inclined to try to oust a Cabinet member anyway.) The probes he likely faces next year could act as a preview of what would happen in 2029 if a Democratic president follows him. Trump enjoys a sort of immunity granted by the Supreme Court, and he has vowed to give preemptive pardons to many people in this administration. Yet advisers say he is unhappy at the prospect of his inner circle facing punishing investigations once he leaves office. [ Read: Here’s who Democrats want to impeach next ] Today’s vote is a clear marker on Trump’s road to irrelevance. Many close to him believe that his driving motivation—more than power or money—is attention. And for a decade now, he has blocked out the sun, dominating the discourse in a way that no other president has in generations. But that will begin to change as Washington begins to look beyond him. Once a colossus, Trump will quickly find himself to be a secondary storyline. It’s not as if he will suddenly vanish; he’ll aim to play GOP kingmaker, and he’ll still surely inspire loyalty from his hard-core believers, even if that group shrinks. He’ll still be commander in chief, and even lame-duck presidents have broad authority when it comes to foreign policy. A return to war with Iran? A move on Cuba? Revisiting Greenland? With Trump fixated on his legacy and desperate to stay in the spotlight, anything feels possible. Trump also may start to see the complete fealty of the Republican Party erode. This stunning midterms wipeout suggests that Trump’s instincts and influence seem to be waning, and Republicans may be more willing to defy him. As the next round of presidential contenders begins to emerge, Republicans will begin to sort out what their post-MAGA future will look like—and what role, if any, Trump plays in it.

items.title: Donald Trump Is Bad at Politics
items.description: L ong before he entered politics, Donald Trump divided humanity into winners and losers, and nothing has mattered more to him than counting himself among the former. This need drove his refusal to accept the 2020 election results—how could a man defined by winning lose? Whatever misgivings some Republicans may have about Trump’s character or his policies, many subscribe to the theory that, if nothing else, the man knows how to win. And his aura of mastery has extended beyond his followers to the Americans who most detest him. The disgust with which many liberals regard Trump is mixed with fear and envy. His powers of persuasion are a source of endless fascination. They have launched a thousand diner safaris to explore his mystical hold on Real America, and inspired innumerable Democratic activists and intellectuals to ponder how they could create a Trump of their own. But Trump is not a winner. He is, for the most part, a loser. In 2016, he lost the national popular vote—that is, the measure of which candidate Americans wanted to win the election—by two percentage points. His party lost control of the House in the 2018 midterms. Trump lost reelection in 2020. His sole unambiguous victory came in 2024, when he faced the clumsy fill-in candidate for an unpopular administration, against which he prevailed, almost by default. And now he has lost again. The 2026 midterm elections are delivering a repudiation of historic magnitude to the president’s party, extending far deeper than the customary pendulum swing against the party in power. Not only did Trump’s presidency as a whole repel the electorate, but also his specific interventions in Republican primaries proved counterproductive. He handpicked Senate candidates, such as Ken Paxton in Texas and Darline Graham in South Carolina, for their loyalty, assuming that any warm body could prevail in such deep-red states. Yet Graham went down to defeat, and Paxton currently trails his Democratic opponent, James Talarico. [ Read: What Donald Trump fears most ] The results help clarify the precise nature of Trump’s political talent. He does possess a certain animal cunning that allows him to home in on human weakness, among both his allies and his targets. (“Jeb’s a loser,” he said in February 2016. “The last thing we need, frankly, is another Bush.”) His speech is so ambiguous and discursive that he avoids being pinned down on particulars. These traits have made him relatively effective as a challenger, exploiting discontent with his opponents while making grand promises (a golden era of wealth, world peace) without specifying any steps he will take to achieve them. None of these skills translates to effective governing. After his election victory two years ago, Democrats feared, and expected, that Trump would coast on the economic recovery he inherited. The post-COVID inflation that had poisoned Joe Biden’s presidency was settling back to normal, and Trump needed only to allow economic gravity to do its work while taking credit for the result. Instead, Trump carried out the wrenching economic changes that he was unable to enact during his first term, in part because he was obstructed by his advisers and by senators from his own party. In 2017, he came one John McCain vote short of defunding the Affordable Care Act, a defeat that spared Trump’s party the political repercussions of stripping health insurance from millions of Americans. In 2025, a more compliant Republican Congress granted him his wish to gut the ACA, along with food stamps, courting the pain they had avoided eight years earlier. After successfully taking advantage of the Biden administration’s failure to contain a surge in migrants, even winning support from millions of Latino voters, Trump proceeded to alienate swing voters with mass deportations carried out through a frequently brutal and occasionally deadly campaign of mass terror. After promising during the 2024 campaign to bring down prices, he took active measures that economists knew would push them higher. Rather than using tariffs mostly as a bluff and settling for modestly rejiggered trade agreements for which he could claim credit, as he did during his first term, he imposed the costliest tariffs since the Herbert Hoover era. When enterprising members of Congress decided, without Trump’s involvement, to pass a bill earlier this year to encourage more housing construction, Trump could have taken credit for their work and demonstrated at least an interest in addressing a major cost driver. Instead, angry that Republicans had failed to pass his bill restricting voting, he petulantly boycotted the signing ceremony. Declining to sign a bipartisan housing bill at a moment when housing costs are a top public concern is the political equivalent of being handed a baby and refusing to kiss it. Most incredible of all, 10 years after he astonished the commentariat by standing on a Republican debate stage in hawkish South Carolina and declaring the Iraq War “a big, fat mistake,” Trump replicated the George W. Bush administration’s signature blunder by launching a war of choice in the Middle East without any plausible exit strategy. Trump might have received a little bit of grace from voters if he had made visible gestures of concern for the pain that Americans felt from these policies. Presidents in the past have grasped the need to show the country that they are working hard, because, if nothing else, regular people typically assume that improving the economy is a function of presidential diligence, like a landlord fixing a leaky toilet. Instead, Trump turned his attention to decorating palaces, erecting monuments, renaming buildings after himself, and demanding awards. He has weirdly inverted a classic populist trope, which posits that the wealth and comfort of the capital comes at the expense of the prosperity of the decent, God-fearing people of the heartland. Trump obsesses in public about his focus on the tiny area in the immediate vicinity of the White House. He devoted his closing message the day before the election to a lengthy recitation of improvements in the capital, from his war against algae to a proposed golf course, which he promised would give residents of Washington a discount. This fixation is a source of pride only for those whose chief goal for this presidency is Trump’s glorification. T he theme connecting all of these baffling choices is a misread of the 2024 election results. The MAGA cult was never large enough to win a majority of the Electoral College. Trump won because he offered an alternative to an unpopular Biden administration, and because enough of the public fondly recalled his first presidential term before COVID struck—and retroactively excused him for the consequences of his pandemic mismanagement. The myth of Trump’s political genius is primarily a by-product of this first-term good fortune. He inherited a healthy economy and had little effect on its trajectory, paradoxically benefiting from failure. The buoyant recovery created a floor beneath his approval ratings that no gaffe or scandal could crash through. Trump, however, convinced himself that he had won because the public shared his conclusion that his first term had been a treacherous betrayal by his enemies. And so, while Trump’s 2024 coalition hinged on Americans who felt nostalgic for his first term, these same voters empowered a president determined not to repeat it. [ David Frum: Only losers play the madman ] He ruthlessly purged the bureaucracy and his party of all dissent so that he could build the dream palace of his imagination—an imperium that would silence his critics in the news media, reduce the business elite to sniveling courtiers, and venerate him as a king. Many of these efforts have met with success. But the unwavering loyalty he has commanded within his party has come at the price of revulsion outside of it. Trump made the autocrat’s error of believing his own propaganda, thus denying himself the benefit of realistic advice that might help him avert or correct his misjudgments. And by treating disagreement as treason, he locked the exits, trapping his fellow Republicans with him as he burned down their reputation. While the Americans who worship Trump as a culture-war champion or god-king remain enthralled, the ones who thought they were hiring him for a four-year gig to get a handle on the border and inflation regard his second term as a failure. Those two constituencies are often conflated with each other, and Republicans have encouraged the conflation by treating his fans as the authentic Volk . In reality, Trump’s base is not synonymous with the country. His base has never constituted anything close to a national majority. Stripped of the protective gloss he enjoyed from the healthy economy during his first term, Trump has no more political magic than Jimmy Carter.

items.title: ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
items.description: South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country’s former ruling party, the African National Congress (ANC). This year’s voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes. Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa’s nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection. For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended. Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime. At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%. Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral. “What I’m seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers,” he told supporters at the party’s final election rally on Sunday. In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support. The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard. Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his vote We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so. They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services. But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change. “We face many challenges in Alexandra. There’s rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues,” he said. Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties. On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road. The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of decline The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn’t vote, even though she is registered to do so. The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision. “It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years,” she said. Alex, as the township is known, is a stone’s throw away from Sandton, Africa’s richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker. Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it. The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships. South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery. Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community’s daily struggles with accessing water and electricity. “Every Monday we know we won’t have water after 2pm,” he said. Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the “arrogance” he says local leaders have towards residents and “change the status quo”. These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa’s local governance. Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa’s 257 municipalities. A recent report only gave 39 clean audits – the highest ranking a public entity can achieve – between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng’s three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list. Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg “needs ongoing attention”. “If we don’t that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living,” she told lawmakers. The city has been labelled “effectively bankrupt” due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years. Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa’s wealthiest city as well as the country’s seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.Of South Africa’s eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party. But that might change. Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a “verdict … and judgment” on the ANC. “And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it’s ever done,” she said. Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday’s election, contested by over 500 political parties. One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC’s support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021. The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time. DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention. The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a “Gusheshe”. She believes the DA is the country’s best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that “towns and cities that work best are under DA governance”. Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa’s ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng. These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities. Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the years Verwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power. Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country’s best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC. Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a “different story”, Verwoerd said. The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won’t and will need partners to form a government. The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election. Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be “very messy” given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA. A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections. Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd’s assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros. “We’re not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run,” he said. Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa’s elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline. Ndou attributed this to the “calibre” of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns. South Africa’s electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

items.title: From Kumasi, a young Ghanaian woman is stitching a new future for African fashion
items.description: Inside a fashion workshop in Sawaba, a suburb of Kumasi, sewing machines hum as young women work on different garments. Some carefully cut fabric, others operate sewing machines, while a few concentrate on decorating dresses with beads, pearls and stones. For some, this is the beginning of a journey into fashion design. For others, it is an opportunity to develop skills they hope will provide an alternative source of income. At the centre of this activity is Bilkis Zulkarnain, a graduate of Kumasi Technical University with a Bachelor of Technology (BTech) in Fashion Design. She wants to make her school a centre for developing female talent beyond Ghana’s borders. Her journey into fashion began with a childhood passion. At social gatherings and other events, people often admired how she dressed. As a Muslim woman, she developed a particular interest in clothing that combined elegance with modesty, which eventually led her to study fashion. She initially launched her own fashion brand, but her industry experience led her to identify what she sees as a missed opportunity for African designers. Despite the continent’s creative talent, many consumers still rely on modest clothing imported from countries such as Turkey, Dubai, and Saudi Arabia. Bilkis believes African designers can produce equally attractive garments and compete in the international market. “When I looked at the modest fashion industry, I realised that although Africa has many talented designers, we still depend heavily on imported modest clothing. I began asking myself why African designers could not produce equally beautiful and competitive designs,” she says. In response, she established Alkiss Fashion School, with the broader ambition of helping African designers move beyond being consumers of international fashion. “I want Africa to become part of the global modest fashion conversation, not just as a consumer, but as a continent that designs, produces, educates and leads. That is one of the reasons I established Alkis Fashion School,” she says. Training women beyond the classroom Bilkis’s ambition also stems from her understanding of the difficulties young women face after university as they struggle to find employment. She believes many graduates become discouraged when formal employment, particularly government jobs, proves difficult to secure, often overlooking the opportunities that practical skills can provide. Having experienced the limitations of academic qualifications without continuous practical development, she wants to help other women build alternative paths to economic independence. “I am passionate about training young women because I am also a young woman. I understand the challenges many of us face, particularly after university when finding a job becomes difficult,” she says. “Some graduates believe that without a government job or formal employment, there is very little they can achieve. I want them to understand that practical skills can also create opportunities,” she added. Since 2023, Bilkis says, she has trained about 120 women in fashion design and garment production. The intention is not just to teach them how to operate sewing machines, but to equip them with the knowledge and confidence to become independent designers and entrepreneurs. For Khadimatullah Suleiman Ishaq, one of the school’s graduates, that opportunity has been life-changing. She says the skills she learned at Alkiss helped her open her own fashion shop, where she now produces garments and trains other aspiring designers. “I am grateful to Allah, and I also want to thank Alkiss Fashion School for everything it has done for me,” she says. “I have benefited tremendously from the training I received at Alkiss. With the knowledge and skills I acquired, and by the grace of Allah, I have been able to establish my own fashion shop. I can now also teach others with confidence,” she further stated. Khadimatullah says she had long wanted to pursue fashion but did not know how to turn that ambition into a business. She credits Bilkis with encouraging her to start small instead of waiting until she had all the resources she thought she needed. “I never imagined I could achieve this much. Fashion had always been my dream, but knowing how to get started was a major challenge,” she says. “She taught me that I did not need to have everything before starting. She encouraged me to begin with just one sewing machine and explained that what mattered most was the effort I put into it.” Khadimatullah says she followed the advice and gradually built her business. She currently has seven students, including two who attend weekend classes. One works with Ghana Water Company, while another works at the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA). Most of her weekday students, she says, enrolled with little or no garment-making experience. “Some had never handled fabric or even used a pair of scissors before. Alhamdulillah, they have now made significant progress. They can independently cut and sew their own dresses and create their own designs without needing my supervision or assistance,” she says. For Bilkis, these experiences reflect the multiplier effect she hopes to achieve: ensuring women acquire skills, establish businesses, and create opportunities for others. A degree is only the beginning Bilkis knows entering the fashion industry requires more than an academic qualification. Her university education provided the foundation, including opportunities to gain additional experience through industrial attachments. However, she says she discovered she needed much more to become fully established in the industry. “My university education gave me the foundation and basic knowledge I needed. We also had industrial attachments where we learnt practical skills. But after completing school, I realised there was still so much more to learn,” she says. “In fashion, you cannot stop learning. The industry keeps evolving, new designs and techniques emerge, and you have to keep upgrading your skills.” She further said. She believes continuous learning is essential for designers who want to stay relevant in an industry where styles, techniques, and customer preferences constantly change. From Togo and The Gambia to Kumasi The school’s ambitions are also attracting students from beyond Ghana. Four women from Mali, Togo, Côte d’Ivoire and The Gambia are currently undertaking fashion training at Alkis Fashion School in Kumasi. Among them are 24-year-old Kambara Houda from Togo and Isatou Mamansa Sanko from The Gambia, who describe their experiences as an opportunity to acquire practical skills they hope to use in their respective countries. For Kambara, the decision to travel from Togo to Ghana was influenced by what she considers the school’s emphasis on practical training. “I believe that learning without putting your knowledge into practice cannot make you a good fashion designer,” she says. She says fashion training in Togo takes longer and offers fewer practical sessions compared with her experience at Alkiss Fashion School. At the Kumasi-based institution, she says, students learn both the theory and practice of fashion design, with opportunities to work on different garments. Her training has included making abaya dresses, including Dubai-style designs, and decorating them with stones, beads, pearls and decorative trims. She has also learnt to cut fabric and make trousers, blazers, hijabs and kimonos. She says the experience has given her skills she hopes to share with other women when she returns home. “I do not want to keep this knowledge to myself. I want to share what I have learnt by teaching other girls and women who are interested in becoming fashion designers,” she says. Isatou Mamansa Sanko, who comes from The Gambia, is also undertaking her first formal fashion design training. She says the six-month programme has provided opportunities to learn different aspects of garment production through practical sessions. Her experience includes making abaya dresses, cutting fabric, and using decorative materials such as pearls, stones, and trims. She has also learnt to make trousers, blazers, hijabs and kimonos. Like Kambara, Isatou hopes to pass on the knowledge she has acquired. “I do not want to keep everything I have learnt to myself. I want to share this knowledge and teach other girls and women who want to become fashion designers. I want them to have the opportunity to learn these skills and develop their abilities,” she says. Their experiences illustrate the potential of practical skills training to create opportunities beyond the country in which the training takes place. For Bilkis, this is an important part of the school’s purpose to equip women who can eventually establish businesses, employ others and transfer their knowledge to their communities. An ambition beyond fashion training The initiative comes at a time when many African countries are grappling with youth unemployment and the challenge of creating economic opportunities for young people. Although fashion training cannot solve these wider problems, Bilkis believes it can open another path for women who struggle to enter the formal job market. Her ambitions for Alkis Fashion School extend beyond Kumasi. She hopes to expand it into a regional training centre that attracts aspiring designers from countries such as Senegal, Nigeria and Liberia, equipping them with the skills to contribute to Africa’s modest fashion industry. Turning that vision into reality, however, will require access to sewing equipment, finance, affordable materials, and reliable markets if graduates are to build businesses that can survive and grow. Bilkis is determined to help create those opportunities. “I want to build a bigger fashion training centre where women from across Africa can come to learn, develop their talents and become independent designers and entrepreneurs,” she says. “I want someone to be able to say that she came to Kumasi, learnt at Alkis Fashion School and returned home to build something of her own. That is the legacy I want to leave,” she adds. For now, that vision is taking shape in a Kumasi workshop, where women from across West Africa are learning to turn fabric into finished garments, with the potential to build livelihoods from the skills they gain.

items.title: Belated meeting
items.description: IT may have taken seven months, but incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan has finally met his lawyer . Meetings between prisoners and their counsel are a right, but the unfortunate fact is that when it comes to the PTI chief, legal requirements have mostly been ignored. The PTI says that Barrister Salman Safdar only discussed legal issues with the former prime minister, and that political matters were not brought up in the brief meeting. Mr Khan’s wife Bushra Bibi was also present. While the decision to allow the PTI chief to consult his counsel is welcome, the state must not think that it has displayed great munificence by granting this access — Mr Khan must be given all the facilities the law sanctions to those in jail. This is all the more imperative following the Supreme Court’s order in August that Mr Khan be allowed to visit a private hospital in Islamabad and consult physicians of his choice. It had also upheld his rights to regular family visits. As the learned court noted, “a prisoner does not … cease to be entitled to humane treatment and necessary medical care”. Yet the government has been highly selective in its interpretation of the court’s orders, taking Mr Khan, instead, to a government health facility, and largely disallowing family visits. In fact, Mr Khan’s sisters were themselves incarcerated under the Maintenance of Public Order in September. They have similarly had great difficulty in meeting family members. Whether it is Mr Khan, his family members, or other incarcerated political leaders and activists, the state should not deny them their rights. These include adequate medical care, family visits, and access to counsel of their choice. The rulers must show basic humanity as well as respect for the Constitution. The PTI, which is currently facing an internal crisis, also needs to eschew its combative rhetoric, and engage with other political actors in order to end the deadlock facing the country, and help salvage the democratic project. Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

He cited executions associated with those foundations as the basis for his position. And I can tell you, the president is not going to cover anyone,” he stated. He said party loyalty would not prevent disciplinary action: “Because we don’t have a problem punishing our members.” Mr Kwetey warned that members unable to meet the required standard could lose their positions. “If you are not capable of doing what is right. items.title: Opposition nominees sought for election reforms panel
items.description: • PTI whip says participation ‘difficult’ following developments in KP • Minister says committee seats to be allocated on basis of strength in NA • PPP blames opposition for delay in appointment of new CEC ISLAMABAD: The government on Tuesday formally approached the opp­o­s­ition to seek its representation on the proposed Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Refo­rms (PCER). How­ever, the opposition termed the formation of the committee a “futile exercise” unless its long-standing demands were met. The committee is being formed to make the electoral process fair, transparent and acceptable to all stakeholders. Federal Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry contacted PTI chief whip in the National Assembly Aamir Dogar, asking him to submit the names of opposition lawmakers for the committee. When contacted, Mr Dogar confirmed that the minister had telephoned him to seek nominations. He said the opposition would hold a meeting to discuss the invitation and the decision would be ann­o­unced by National Asse­mbly Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai. Questioning how the opposition could join the committee under the prevailing circumstances, Mr Dogar referred to the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the alleged detention of the provincial chief minister and the arrest of more than 10 PTI leaders. He also alleged that the PTI’s mandate had been stolen in the last general elections. “How can the government expect the opposition to sit with it on the committee under these circumstances?” he asked. Mr Dogar also expressed reservations over the proposed composition of the committee and demanded equal representation for the government and opposition. Meanwhile, PTI’s interim Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan told reporters that the opposition would not oppose the committee if the dialogue was conducted sincerely. The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), a major ally of the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), has already approached opposition leaders Mehmood Khan Achakzai in the National Assembly and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas in the Senate, inviting them to join the proposed committee. However, Mr Chaudhry said the committee was an initiative of National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, not the PPP. He said that if the opposition agreed to join, it would have to submit the names of its representatives to the speaker. Explaining the formula for representation, the minister said one committee seat would be allocated for every 16 members of the National Assembly. On Monday, Mr Chaudhry contacted the ruling coalition’s allies and wrote separate letters to the PPP and MQM-P chief whips in the National Assembly, Ijaz Jakhrani and Aminul Haq, respectively, seeking nominations. Under the proposed formula, the PML-N would have nine members, the PPP five and the MQM-P one, he said. The minister said smaller parties allied with the ruling coalition did not qualify for representation under the agreed criteria. The PML-N had therefore decided to allocate one seat each to its smaller allies, including the Balochistan Awami Party (BAP) and Pakistan Muslim League-Zia (PML-Z), from its quota of nine seats. He urged the opposition to join the committee, saying the initiative could also pave the way for consultations on other important national issues, including the long-delayed appointment of a new chief election commissioner (CEC). CEC appointment Meanwhile, PPP leader Naveed Qamar blamed the opposition for the delay in appointing a new CEC. Speaking to DawnNewsTV ’s Nadir Guramani, he said the appointment of a new CEC would benefit the opposition, which had repeatedly questioned the role of incumbent CEC Sikandar Sultan Raja. He said that under the 26th Constitutional Amendment, the incumbent CEC would continue to serve despite the expiry of his term until a successor was appointed. “We have also expressed displeasure to opposition leader Mehmood Achakzai for not meeting the prime minister under a constitutional requirement to hold consultations on the appointment of a new chief election commissioner. The opposition leader should not say that he cannot sit with the PM here or there,” he said. “I think the ball is now in the opposition’s court as it has to remove all hurdles coming in the process of appointment of a new chief election commissioner,” he added. Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

items.title: Electoral reform
items.description: THE parliamentary committee on electoral reform , which is being constituted by the National Assembly Speaker, sounds promising. But the public has watched this exercise many times before. None has delivered a credible election. Therefore, the legislators must ask why the laws already on the books keep failing before they start redrafting new statutes. Pakistan’s current electoral framework appears to be sound. The Election Commission of Pakistan enjoys constitutional protection, financial autonomy, and a bipartisan process for appointing its leadership. Yet both the 2018 and 2024 general elections ended in bitter disputes over the credibility and transparency of results. Neither the government nor the opposition has made a serious effort to initiate consultations on a replacement for the current chief election commissioner whose tenure ended nearly two years ago. The real problem is the gulf between the statute book and what happens on polling day, not the laws. Legitimacy depends on consistent enforcement, genuine institutional independence, and a shared willingness to respect the rules. Nevertheless, the committee can still close several gaps in the current legislation. First, provinces routinely delay local government elections for years, citing the need to amend local laws. This stops the ECP from discharging its constitutional duty when the term of an elected LG expires. Parliament should bar provincial governments from altering local election laws once a council completes its tenure, so that the ECP can hold polls within the constitutional time frame. Second, campaign finance rules are full of loopholes. Under the Elections Act, 2017, candidates can dodge spending limits by claiming that third-party expenditure was not authorised by their campaigns. Spending limits mean little if a candidate can disown whoever spends on their behalf. If money is spent to advance a candidate’s campaign, the candidate should answer for it. Third, financial scrutiny must be extended to foreign funding to both parties and individual candidates routed through affiliated non-profits and offshore accounts for the sake of transparency. Last but not least, the caretaker government model needs an overhaul. Letting political parties haggle over nominees does not guarantee neutrality, which must be tested against the record of those appointed. The law should have clearer safeguards against conflicts of interest and political bias among caretaker officeholders, so that transitions are not open to partisan interference. These fixes are worth making. But they will count for little if meddling in polls and selective enforcement continue to be unchecked. Domestic and international observers raised serious concerns about the 2024 results process. Until parliament deals with the interference that feeds public distrust, further amendments will change very little. The country does not need a new rulebook. It needs institutions and actors who follow the one it already has. Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

Il s’agit d’Achraf Hakimi (Paris Saint-Germain), Nayef Aguerd (Olympique de Marseille) et Yassine Gessime (Strasbourg), récompensés pour leurs prestations remarquées. Achraf Hakimi a signé la performance la plus marquante. Le latéral du PSG a obtenu la note maximale de 10/10 après un match exceptionnel face au Havre, remporté par les Parisiens sur le score de 5-1. Enfin, Yassine Gessime s’est lui aussi distingué avec une note de 10/10. Sous les couleurs de Strasbourg, il a participé à la victoire 5-1 contre Auxerre en inscrivant deux buts et en délivrant une passe décisive. Avec ces trois distinctions, les joueurs marocains signent une présence remarquée dans l’équipe type de cette neuvième journée de Ligue 1.
